articleTitle: Don’t interfere with ‘right to azaan’ at mosque if noise norms followed: Allahabad HC
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Saharanpur
description: Petitioners claim authorities were not allowing them to use loudspeakers for azaan despite court orders allowed it
body_raw: The Allahabad High Court has directed the authorities concerned to not interfere with the right to five-time azaan Islamic call for a prayer at a mosque in Saharanpur district, provided the noise pollution rules are complied with strictly. A writ petition was filed in the court in July requesting to direct the district administration and police to permit the mosque management to perform azaan five times at Ayesha Masjid in Pathed village of Gagalhedi area and permit the use of loudspeakers for the purpose. According to the petitioners, despite there being court judgments permitting the use of loudspeakers for azaan, the authorities were not allowing them to do so. The state governments counsel, however, submitted before the bench that the petitioners were not restrained from performing azaan as such but were only asked to use loudspeaker according to the Noise Pollution Regulation and Control Rules, 2000, which provide for certain level of sound in terms of decibel units. Citing a May 2020 Allahabad High Court judgment, the counsel maintained that certain timings have also been prescribed for the use of loudspeakers for the purpose of azaan. The 2020 judgment stated that azaan may be an integral part of Islam but the call through loudspeakers or other sound amplifying devices cannot be an essential part of the religion, warranting protection of the fundamental right under Article 25 of the Constitution. Therefore, under no circumstances sound amplifying devices can be permitted to be used between 10 pm and 6 am by the district administrations, it was stated. The 2020 order also maintained that in case any such application is filed before the authorities concerned, it may be dealt with in accordance with law, including noise pollution norms. The petitioners submitted that there was no question of violating any rule or the court order on the use of loudspeakers and their use during azaan will be followed strictly. After hearing the submissions, the division bench of Justices Ajit Kumar and Garima Prashad in its October 1 order directed the petitioners to file an affidavit to comply with the Noise Pollution Regulation and Control Rules, 2000, as well as the HCs 2020 order. It will however, be the duty of the police as well as district administration to ensure that the petitioners do abide by their own undertaking given in the affidavit, failing which it will remain open for them to take appropriate action in accordance with law, the bench stated.

articleTitle: Amid heat and pollution, BMC prunes gardens budget even as 200 wait for repairs
articleFeaturedImageAlt: mahalaxmi race course
description: Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) records show that the budget allocated for the civic body’s garden and trees department, which is responsible for developing and maintaining the city’s green cover, has seen a consistent decline over the past five years.
body_raw: Mumbai is grappling with intense heat and poor air, but the citys most natural defence against both - green and open spaces - appears to be constrained by a severe funding crunch. Records accessed by The Indian Express show that at present, there is a requirement to construct and repair as many as 200 gardens and open spaces in Mumbai. However, the work couldnt be taken up due to financial crunch. Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation BMC records show that the budget allocated for the civic bodys garden and trees department, which is responsible for developing and maintaining the citys green cover, has seen a consistent decline over the past five years. According to the records, the BMC has received around 210 requests from elected representatives, including MLAs and corporators, for creating gardens, recreational grounds and playgrounds across Mumbai. Our department garden and tree has received requests for work worth Rs 710 crore. Since many of the requests are non-feasible and cant be executed on immediate basis, a technical assessment was carried out. It was found that the basic work in many of these gardens requires a funding of Rs 250 crore, an official told The Indian Express on the condition of anonymity. This amount is more than three times the Rs 68-crore budget allocated for the trees and gardens department for the current financial year. Costly affair Officials said the process of creating an open space is a multi-step method. After a land parcel is given to the BMC by the collectors office or the land and revenue department, the first step involves making the soil component fertile for grass plantation. Then utilities such as furniture, gym and playing apparatus along with compound walls are erected. Officials said that as a whole, the cost of constructing a new garden from scratch costs Rs 25-30 crore, while the cost of carrying out basic repair works costs Rs 4-5 crore as per the current rates. There are many gardens in Mumbai where no repair works have been taken up in a decade. In our latest survey, we found that there are recreational grounds where the walkways are broken, apparatus are stolen and toilets are defunct. Many of these spaces are either encroached or shut to the public, the official said. He also added that most of these gardens are located in wards M East Govandi, Deonar, M west Chembur, S Kanjurmarg and Bhandup, L Kurla and K North Jogeshwari. Most of these house the middleclass population. Budget constraints The civic bodys data shows that the budget allocated for the garden and tree department has fallen by 62 per cent in the past three years. For the financial year 2023-24, the BMC had earmarked Rs 180.83 crore for this department. However, the final budget for the garden department for this year stands at Rs 68 crore, against Rs 200 crore proposed in the budget earlier this year. The final budget for the garden and tree department was cut down by 66 per cent in the final allocation as part of it was routed towards infrastructure works, another official told The Indian Express. Budget documents also show that five key infrastructure projects have accounted for 42 per cent of the overall capital expenditure. These projects include BMCs waste water treatment facility WWTF under which the civic body aims to construct seven sewage treatment plants STP, the ongoing road concretising project, the Mumbai Coastal Road North Versova-Dahisar project, the Goregaon Mulund Link Road GMLR project and the BMCs water conveyance tunnel project. We understand that there has been a shortfall in allocation, but one has to realise that the budget estimates were prepared before the elected representatives occupied offices in BMC, according to Ganesh Khankar, leader of the house and Bharatiya Janata Party BJP corporator. We are in talks with the administration to scale up the allocation to the gardens department by 25-30 per cent for this year and correct it further next year, Khankar said. Opposition cries foul Leaders from Opposition parties said that their requests for creating new gardens are either being withheld or being sent back by the administration. Congress corporator and group leader Ashraf Azmi had sent a letter in June demanding repair works in six gardens in his constituency, Kurla. However, he didnt receive any response. In a follow-up letter in September, Azmi wrote, The jogging tracks in the park are in poor condition and the walls are in a state of collapse. The slides, swings and other materials for children have been dilapidated. In a similar letter, Shiv Sena UBT corporator Sachin Padwal requested an upgradation of a garden at Kalachowky. He is yet to get a response. Why open spaces are important Mumbai is one of the space starved cities in the world and according to civic records, the ratio of open space stands at 0.87 square metre per person, while the World Health Organisation WHO recommends that every human being should have access to 9 square meters of open space. In 2022, the union ministry of Housing and urban affairs MoHUA recommended that in India the ratio of open space should be 10-12 square meters per person. The Urban Regional Development Plans Formulation and Implementation URDPFI guidelines, 2014 recommend 10 to 12 sqm of open space per person. State and Union territories, urban development authorities and urban local bodies are expected to adopt the URDPFI guidelines in accordance with prevailing local conditions which may vary from city to city, a MoHUA statement read. Earlier this year, the BMC awarded the work of developing and maintaining a 70 hectare stretch of open space adjoining Mumbais coastal road to the Reliance group. Sources said that the Mahalaxmi Racecourse, which has been taken over by the BMC in 2024, is also likely to be developed and maintained by a private entity under corporate social responsibility CSR drive. The fact that BMC has a small budget for open spaces, clearly shows that the agency is working towards privatising open spaces. In cases like this, universal access to these spaces are usually restricted which equates, for those who are denied access, to not having an open spaces, said Hussain Indorewala, urban planner and researcher. Topographic challenges In August, during an interaction with The Indian Express editorial team, Mumbais municipal commissioner Ashwini Bhide said that considering the citys landmass and topography, the per capita green space is more than enough. As city planners, we need to strike a balance with the reality of Mumbai. We have around 30 to 32 lakh trees in the city, when we include trees from Aarey forest. Out of that 2 lakh trees are along the road. This number is good, but equitable distribution is an issue. But, we can do better, Bhide said. I fully understand that we need more open spaces. But in a city where the land itself is a scarcity, we have to be very innovative in terms of creating spaces. Maybe our buildings should utilise its podium area and create open spaces, she said.

articleTitle: 5 injured in accident on Pune-Mumbai Expressway’s Missing Link; traffic diverted briefly
articleFeaturedImageAlt: pune mumbai accident
description: According to the State Highway Police, the injured have been provided with necessary medical assistance.
body_raw: At least five people were injured after a private bus collided with a container on the Pune-Mumbai Expressways Missing Link Connecting Link on Tuesday morning. The injured have been provided with necessary medical assistance, State Highway Police said. The incident led to the closure of the Pune-to-Mumbai carriageway, with traffic being briefly diverted through the Ghat section of the expressway. Traffic movement towards Mumbai remained closed on the carriageway for four to five hours before being restored by afternoon as the damaged vehicles were removed from the spot. The State Highway Police confirmed that the situation was under control. The accident also brought into focus the restrictions on and violations by the vehicles on the Connecting Link. Containers are not permitted on the Missing Link, while buses are allowed to use the corridor. The container involved in the accident was therefore in violation of the restrictions applicable to the route. The Highway Police said official, detailed information about the circumstances of the accident will be shared after an initial probe. Motorists travelling from Pune towards Mumbai have been advised to follow the directions of the traffic police and use the Ghat section until the affected carriageway is cleared and reopened.

articleTitle: Ajay Devgn’s Drishyam 3 reminds us that more than family, the franchise is about movies
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Ajay Devgn's Vijay Salgaonkar tells a story throughout the Drishyam trilogy.
description: Ajay Devgn's Drishyam 3 concludes on a high, unlike the far more family-oriented Malayalam version, because it ties in neatly with what's always been the franchise's spiritual fulcrum -- the movies.
body_raw: More than a standalone movie, Abhishek Pathaks Drishyam 3 works best as the third act of Drishyam, if it were a consolidated crime thriller instead of a trilogy. The conflict gets set in Nishikant Kamats first part 2020 when Sam dies at the hands of Vijay Salganonkars Ajay Devgn family. The plot thickens in Pathaks Drishyam 2 2022 before the resolution comes in at a cinematic high in Drishyam The Conclusion, which released this past Friday on the befitting date of October 2. Like for the Goa police, pav bhaji, Maharaj ji ka satsang, and film watching in Panjim which film did they watch? Drishyam 3? were all distractions even for the audience. All this while, unreliable narrator Salgaonkar was doing what he does best - telling us a story through drishyam visuals. The movie-watching underdog In the first Drishyam, were introduced to Vijay Salgaonkar, a fourth class dropout whose only means to securing an education has been watching movies. Hes particularly on a steady diet of thrillers. Theyve edited it with fast cuts and taking the audience for a ride. On top of that is the pounding music So that it seems a lot is going on. But nothing is really happening. You need to feel the tension, he tells his subordinate, probably also referring to the Drishyam trilogy that takes its own sweet time to lure the audience in. At one point, Salgaonkar is also seen watching and weeping to Vipul Shahs 2005 family drama Waqt The Race Against Time. Though thats far from being a crime thriller, it does sound like a tagline to the Drishyam franchise itself. Because as the films unfold, we realize that every step of the way, Salgaonkar was far ahead of anyone else in the race against time. After his family panics following the murder of Sam, the only son of Goa Police Inspector General Meera Deshmukh Tabu, Salgaonkar devises a foolproof plan. He takes his family for an outing in Panjim the next day in order to crystallize the same chronology in granular detail when the police eventually interrogates them. Not just that, he even lives out that delayed reality for all the other eyewitnesses involved - the restaurant owner and the cinema projector operator among others - so that their testimonies sync with those of his family. Since Indians all across have grown up on movies, he uses that very device of visual memory as his weapon of choice. So, when the first part ends, Salgaonkar has an upper hand. But like most sequels, the conflict is brought back with a new lens. Enter Akshaye Khanna, who takes over the case from Tabu, capitalizing on his objective gaze sans personal prejudice. But to Salgaonkar, hes not the chief antagonist, but yet another actor just playing his part ironic, since thats what it turned out to be, given Khannas sudden exit from the franchise before Drishyam 3. To make the stakes more implausible yet interesting, he brings in Saurabh Shuklas character, an author who churns out a book out of the chain of events Salgaonkar has preempted. When the court dismisses the states case against Salgaonkar on the argument that the police is trying to frame a common man and his family by recreating events of a book, that twist seems far too convenient and far-fetched. But Shuklas author character is brought back again in Drishyam 3 to explain the rationale communicated to him by Salgaonkar - Films need not to be real. They just need to seem and feel real. That then becomes the spiritual fulcrum of not only the threequel, but also the trilogy. Suddenly, as Drishyam 3 draws to a close, the audience realize that Salgaonkar had been pulling the puppet strings all along. He uses the fame he gains from the events in the first part to rise the ranks and become a theatre owner from a DVD store owner. The events of the sequel allow him to further gain traction in his career, and become a film producer. But little do we know hes been producing a film all along - the film that weve been watching for the past 11 years. Through whats described as Salgaonkars three-part chakravyuh, the audience gradually uncovers that the sequel wasnt actually the second act, but the beginning of the second half of the film thats Drishyam. The climax of the first part boats of the cinematic high and narrative clencher of the interval block, and Drishyam 2 is merely a stepping stone to the rousing conclusion in Drishyam 3. Like every time, Salgaonkar was way ahead in the game, planning his course of action in Drishyam 2 itself, instead of saving it for the epic conclusion. A step above Mohanlals Drishyam 3 Spoiler alert Till the first two parts, Devgns Drishyam remained mostly faithful to its original source material, Jeetu Josephs films Drishyam and Drishyam 2 respectively, starring Mohanlal as Georgekutty, the Malayalam counterpart of Vijay Salgaonkar. But after the Malayalam Drishyam 3 didnt live up to the hype, Pathak and Devgn changed the course of their franchise, taking a completely new direction. However, this new direction neatly ties in with the spirit of the first part. It also weaves in the polarizing reaction towards Malayalam Drishyam 3 to tell a slightly deceptive story about family. Pathaks Drishyam 3 begins with Rajat Kapoors character Mahesh Deshmukh vowing to reopen the case and put Salgaonkar behind the bars, after his wife Meera tries to end her life out of depression. When Jaideep Ahlawats DCP hits back at Mahesh, asking him if hes a servant who reopens the case at his beck and call, its also a dig at the Malayalam Drishyam 3 which takes too many swings to take the story forward. In that version, Siddique who plays the Malayalam counterpart of Mahesh turns evil, a far cry from the fairly balanced sympathizer he is in the first two parts. Since SalgaonkarGeorgekuttys purported narrative throughout the franchise has been about protecting the family, it makes narrative sense to have another father determined to protect his family by avenging the death of his son. So, when Siddiques character steps up, it shouldve made for a riveting clash of the patriarchs. But what follows is a long-drawn, unwarranted climactic twist in which Georgekutty beats up his daughter in order to frame a troublesome cop. His argument was simple - beating up his daughter was in the larger interest of protecting his family from conviction. But it was not only problematic to watch, but also felt like a melodramatic copout. Surely, when the audience enter a theatre, they want to immerse themselves in the emotion and the drama. But not at the cost of the films own voice. So, when Pathaks Drishyam 3 avoids going down that path and instead pays a tribute to the movies, it all makes complete sense. When Salgaonkar pulls out his final trick from the hat, and the skeletons in his closet come tumbling out pun intended, he underlines what the Drishyam franchise has always been about - movies. Yes, family is at its heart too, but when his wife Nandini Shriya Saran breaks out of the character of the hapless wife, the film exposes family as just a visual decoy to make the police - and the audience - forget that Salgaonkars superhero power is watching movies. As the Malayalam Drishyam 3 revealed, family in fact turns out to be Georgekuttys Kryptonite. While he manages to get his family to dodge conviction yet again - paving the path ahead for another part - it comes at the cost of not only his daughters injuries, but also the audiences dissatisfaction. By making his Drishyam 3 all about the movies, Pathak underscores that while a family man may often have to sacrifice a part of his conscience for the sake of his family, a cinephiles win is written in the movie stars. Whether its a thriller like Drishyam or a family drama like Waqt, its always the sacrificial patriarch who pays a heavy price, while the underdog movie buff wins the race against time.

articleTitle: ‘I don’t call myself a rockstar anymore’: Rhiti Tiwari on being schooled by Salman Khan
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rhiti Tiwari Bigg Boss 20 eviction interview
description: In an exclusive interview, evicted Bigg Boss 20 contestant Rhiti Tiwari recalled Salman Khan schooling her for two hours after she misbehaved with Qazi Touqeer.
body_raw: Manoj Tiwaris daughter, singer Rhiti Tiwari exited Bigg Boss 20 last week following a mid-week eviction. Since leaving the house, Rhiti has been reflecting on her journey on the Salman Khan-hosted reality show. In an exclusive conversation with SCREEN, she opened up about her time on Bigg Boss Season 20, being schooled by Salman over her behaviour, dealing with the nepo kid tag on the show, and the trauma she has faced in her personal life. Rhiti Tiwari on the nepo-kid tag Ever since Rhiti Tiwari entered Bigg Boss 20, a section of the internet has claimed that she landed a spot on the show because of her father Manoj Tiwaris recommendation. Even inside the house, Rhiti had to deal with the nepo kid tag. Reacting to it, Rhiti said, What is really funny is that my dad didnt even know I was going on the show until 1-2 days before. He sent me a news link asking if I was going. If people think I was on the show because of him, thats not true. Sharing her take on nepotism, Rhiti added, I can defend the nepo kid tag, but nepotism holds a different value for me. Before all of this happened and I entered a room, they would know whose daughter I am. There was already love, admiration, and some respect coming to me. Whatever he has earned in his life comes to me as a blessing in terms of respect. If I were truly a nepo-kid, what have I been doing for 5 years? Why didnt I reach the place I aspire to be at? Why is all this happening now? Using his name, I could have done a lot of things, but I wanted to do things myself. I was told you have to do it yourself, so where is the nepotism? Rhiti Tiwari on her equation and fight with Qazi Touqeer Rhiti Tiwari also opened up about her equation with Qazi Touqeer, revealing that she had initially formed a strong emotional bond with the singer. However, after learning that Qazi had faked his illness on the show, Rhiti admitted that she felt deceived and took it personally. She also expressed regret over losing her temper and lashing out at him. I genuinely connected with Qaziji in the beginning. Our artiste-to-artiste energy matched. I doubted if he acted, then we had a deep conversation where I cried. I felt bad about what he was going through. I have built a very strong connection with him. Due to my personal experiences, when I see someone go through something, I get really affected. When I found out it was all for entertainment, I took it personally. He fooled me and hurt my ego. In that fit, I did and said things I wholeheartedly regret. I dont wish to be that person ever again. However, Rhitis anger did not end there. During another task, she used derogatory language against Qazi and even threatened him. Following the incident, Salman Khan schooled Rhiti over her behaviour and told her that she appeared insecure about Qazi. Talking about it, Rhiti said, I wanted the earth to swallow me. I was called insecure, jealous, desperate, and whatnot. I dont call myself a rockstar anymore. I would like the world to call me that one day if they see fit. It was the most ashamed I ever felt. I always thought love and anger were two very strong emotions, but that day I realised what strong emotions like shame, guilt, and embarrassment are. I was weighed down by it. I told myself, What have you done. I was disappointed in myself this was not the Rhiti I came to be. I broke down. I was destroyed. The only way was to rebuild stronger and harder. I took it all. Somewhere, a part of me has not healed from the things I have been through. It came out in all the wrong ways. That house has healed in me, what could have taken 10 years and countless therapy sessions. Everything that happened was my worst fear. Also Read Salman Khan schools Rhiti Tiwari You are Manoj Tiwaris daughter, not Dolly Bindras Asked whether she felt Salman Khan had been a little too harsh on her, Rhiti added, If Salman sir took 2 hours to explain something to me, so that I can be a better human being, I think its my greatest privilege. The whole episode was about me thats insane. I dont think I would have wanted to be called Dolly Bindras daughter. But my actions were such that, obviously, people will comment. Rhiti on parents divorce and trauma During her stint on Bigg Boss 20, Rhiti Tiwari spoke several times about her parents divorce and how the experience continues to affect her. Opening up about growing up in a broken home, Rhiti said, Being from a broken home does affect me. A lot of people from broken homes exist in this world. The things I have seen in life have shaped me. There are things that have not made sense to me yet. A lot of what I did, the way I acted, came from the lack of dealing with and learning about myself. I believe I have been learning, trying to be better, grow, but when you come from these things, they stay in your brain a certain way. When all of this happened to me on Bigg Boss, it healed a very big part of me. Rhiti also spoke about her equation with father Manoj Tiwari today. She said, I am always cheering for my father. If he calls me for support on his show Pati Patni Aur Panga 2, Rhiti Tiwari shall be there for Manoj Tiwari. Today our equation is very loving. We were not able to be around each other a lot I have not lived with him. Whatever happened, he is a proud father I am a proud daughter, and whenever I need him, he is there. On the work front, Rhiti Tiwari is gearing up to release her music album Rejected, which will reflect on her journey on Bigg Boss, her actions and her path to redemption. Explaining the idea behind the album, Rhiti said, I was always someone who felt the most likeable in a room all delusions about myself were shattered on Bigg Boss 20. I was rejected in that house, and I own it.

articleTitle: Drishyam 3 Box Office Collection Day 4 Highlights: Ajay Devgn film grosses Rs 303 cr, set for further drop on Tuesday
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Drishyam 3 Box Office Collection Day 4
description: The worldwide gross of Ajay Devgn-starrer Drishyam The Conclusion currently stands at Rs 303 crore.
body_raw: After a record-breaking opening weekend, Ajay Devgns Drishyam The Conclusion witnessed a sharp drop at the box office on its first Monday. On Day 4, the film earned Rs 21 crore net from 16,274 shows, marking a 65.6 per cent drop from its Sunday collection of Rs 61 crore. This took the films India net collection to Rs 197 crore and domestic gross to Rs 237 crore. Its worldwide gross currently stands at Rs 303 crore. On Day 4, Drishyam The Conclusion recorded an overall Hindi occupancy of 24.71 per cent. articleTitle: Extreme heat puts pregnant women, newborns at greater risk: Survey
articleFeaturedImageAlt: heat, pregnant women
description: Global survey includes 200 Indian maternal healthcare professionals; separate India research examines heat exposure and pregnancy outcomes
body_raw: Extreme heat is increasingly affecting pregnant women and newborns, with maternal healthcare professionals reporting a rise in heat-related complications and growing concerns over health-system preparedness, according to a new international survey commissioned by Wellcome, a global charitable foundation that funds health and scientific research. The survey of 1,000 healthcare professionals across India, Australia, Brazil, the UK and Zimbabwe found that 73 per cent reported an increase in heat-related cases or complications affecting pregnant women over the past five years, while 76 per cent reported an increase affecting foetal or newborn health. Nearly all respondents said they had personally cared for a pregnant woman 98 per cent or baby 99 per cent whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat. India accounted for 200 respondents in the survey, which included obstetricians, gynaecologists, doctors, midwives, nurses and other frontline healthcare workers involved in pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal or newborn care. The survey was conducted online between September 17 and October 1. Separate India-specific research has highlighted the potential consequences of heat exposure during pregnancy. In a July 2026 overview of heat and maternal health, researchers in India had found that working in high heat can double the risk of miscarriage and stillbirth. A separate research is examining the effects of extreme heat on maternal, placental, foetal and newborn health across different climatic regions of India. The study is examining heat exposure during pregnancy and its potential impact on outcomes for mothers and babies, including through research involving 600 pregnant women across three climate zones. Pregnant and postpartum women face particular risks from extreme heat. The study has linked heat exposure with preterm birth, low birth weight, stillbirth and maternal complications. For every 1C rise in heat exposure, the odds of preterm birth increase by around 5 per cent, while exposure to heatwaves has been associated with a 25 per cent higher risk of obstetric complications. Among healthcare professionals surveyed, 23 per cent said they had seen pregnancy complications requiring additional monitoring or treatment that they believed were linked to extreme heat. They also reported low birth weight or restricted growth 34 per cent, dehydration and heat-related illness in newborns 36 per cent, and difficulties with feeding, breathing and temperature regulation 33 per cent. Heat is also affecting access to healthcare. Twenty-seven per cent of respondents said extreme heat was making it harder for pregnant women and families to travel to or access care, while 29 per cent reported an increase in urgent or emergency presentations. Midwives and doctors from countries across five continents are telling us that extreme heat is affecting the health of pregnant women and newborn babies, said Julia Gillard, Chair of Wellcome and former Prime Minister of Australia. As the planet continues to heat-up because of anthropogenic climate change more mothers and babies will be put at risk. More than four in five respondents 81 per cent were concerned that extreme heat would pose a growing risk to maternal, foetal and newborn health over the next five years unless further action is taken. Another 82 per cent said policymakers and health-system leaders should give greater priority to protecting pregnant women and babies from extreme heat. The survey also highlighted a preparedness gap among health workers. Ninety-two per cent of respondents said they wanted more training and resources to protect pregnant women during extreme heat, while 55 per cent said clearer national or international guidance would help them provide better care. Extreme heat, fuelled by climate change is impacting our way of life and our health - and yet many countries are not prepared, said Dr Madeleine Thomson, Head of Climate Impacts and Adaptation at Wellcome. She said measures such as early warning systems and cooler buildings could help protect vulnerable groups, including pregnant women and newborns. The researchers called for pregnant women, new mothers and babies to be specifically included in national climate and health plans, along with clinical guidance on heat during pregnancy and the postpartum period. They have also called for stronger surveillance systems to track the impact of heat exposure on maternal and newborn health. The survey has been released ahead of COP31, as climate and health researchers push for maternal and newborn health to be given greater prominence in climate adaptation and health planning.

articleTitle: India’s bullet train not delayed, even Japan can’t do it in 10 yrs: High-speed rail body head
articleFeaturedImageAlt: India bullet train
description: The official said even though Japan has 62 years of experience in building and operating bullet trains, it cannot complete a 500-km long stretch in 10 years
body_raw: Amid allegations over delays in Indias first bullet train project between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, the head of the international high speed rail body said it should not be said that the project is delayed given the many unforeseen problems India encountered, such as the Covid-19 pandemic and land acquisition. Speaking to The Indian Express on the sidelines of the Kautilya Economic Conclave, Masafumi Shukuri, Chairman of the Japan Transport and Tourism Research Institute JTTRI and International High-Speed Rail Association IHRA, defended the Indian government, saying that even though Japan has 62 years of experience in building and operating bullet trains, it cannot complete a 500-km long stretch in 10 years. The first high-speed rail project in Japan was launched in 1964, which means Japan has 62 years of experience of constructing and operating the high-speed train. Now, lets just say today Japan decides to make a high-speed rail track of 500 km. It is not possible to complete it in 10 years. Even todays Japan cannot do it. I think from this perspective, given the different conditions, building a high-speed rail of 500 km long in India is a big deal, Shukuri said. We also have to remember that initially when any project starts, there are many unforeseen problems. I know that there was a delay in land acquisition and many other things which have to be factored in, the IHRA Chairman added. Shukuris comments come after Hideki Makihara, a former justice minister and a member of Japans ruling Liberal Democratic Party, who alleged in July that India had displayed sheer recklessness in its bullet train project that stalled its progress. The Mumbai-Ahmedabad High Speed Rail MAHSR, Indias first ever bullet train project, was initially expected to be completed in 2022. I do not think there is a delay really, because you have to look at the size of this project. It is a 500 km long alignment. It is being done for the first time in India. With all of this together, it is a humongous, massive project. It is not a project which is expected to be wrapped up and completed in a matter of just a few years. It is just not possible, Shukuri said. Another thing is that we also had to deal with the Covid-19 pandemic, which came with disruption that it took time to get back on track. I feel that despite all of that this project is proceeding very strongly, he further said, adding that IHRA has been involved with the project since 2014, even before it was officially announced. The first section from Surat to Vapi in Gujarat of the 508-km project is scheduled to begin operation by the end of 2027. The entire project is expected to be completed by 2029. The priority section will begin the operation with India-made bullet trains, since the Japanese E10 Shinkansen wont arrive before 2034 and is still under design in Japan. India is currently developing its own bullet train set B28. The design speed of the train is 280 kmph and two sets are being developed by BEML in Bengaluru. It will operate at a maximum speed of 250 kmph. The manufacturing of the train is scheduled to be completed by April 2027, with testing to be done between May-July 2027. The commercial operation of the train will begin by December 2027. Shukuri also said that while it is absolutely fine that India has decided to use its own rolling stock, or India-made bullet train, for the project, it has to ensure the operation is not only stable, but safe and reliable. I think it is not only about procurement of rolling stock and signalling systems. It is also about making sure that training of the people is in place on time, they have the requisite skill-set, they have the technical know-how, as well as enough trials are done to really get a full performance of the final commissioning of the train, said Shukuri. In the Mumbai-Ahmedabad project, three systems were to be taken from the Japanese the Shinkansen bullet train, the Signalling System, and the Operation Control Centre OCC. However, this is yet to be finalised between both countries. The civil construction work is to be done by India.

articleTitle: Only 9% of Indians take public transport to work, buses key for women
articleFeaturedImageAlt: free bus travel
description: More than a fifth of urban women travel to work by bus, three times as high as their male counterparts.
body_raw: The statistics ministrys first-ever household travel survey has found that only 9 of Indians primarily use public transport to go to work, with 43 using two-wheelers. A mere 3 use cars. The surveys results also seemingly back the decision by several states to offer free bus travel to women, with more than a fifth of urban women using this mode of transport to go to work, three times as high as urban men. Further, people in urban areas spend as much as Rs 1,044 per month to commute to work, 71 more than the Rs 612 spent by people in rural areas. Nationally, the average monthly expenditure to go to work is Rs 785. As per the survey, buses are the primary mode of transport for 6.7 of people who reported travelling more than 1 kilometre to reach their place of work. Another 2.1 said they used monorail or tram, while 0.2 said they travel by rail. While monorail, metro, suburban rail, and trams account for 5 of urban worker commutes nationally, usage surges in Maharashtra 20.7, West Bengal 16.5, and Delhi 14.4, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation MoSPI said on Monday. Train, monorail, and tram includes metro rail and local trains. The findings of the National Household Travel Survey NHTS, conducted from July 2025 to June 2026, are based on responses from 20 lakh people across 14,274 villages and 10,377 urban blocks. MoSPI said the surveys main objective is to generate data-driven insights that can be used in regional transport planning and infrastructure developments as well as identify gaps, optimise transport routes, and improve service frequency and scheduling. Free bus travel for women The surveys results back the decision made by several states to offer free bus travel for women, with 21.7 of urban women who travel more than 1 km for work primarily using a bus. For urban males, this figure is just 6.9. In certain states, the fraction of urban women commuting to work by bus was significantly higher than the national average 46.8 in Keralam, 41.1 in Tamil Nadu, 34.9 in Karnataka, and 28.9 in Telangana. The bus category includes public, private, company, and inter-city buses. According to an April 2026 IIT Bombay paper titled Ticket to Ride Impact of free public transport on womens workforce participation in India, participation of women in the labour force is closely linked to access to affordable public transport. In areas where regressive social norms serve as a binding constraint against womens mobility and their workforce participation, the free bus scheme for all women encourages higher ridership which provides a social cover for even more women to travel, thereby starting a virtuous cycle, the paper said, adding that its findings showed that states can leverage the free bus scheme for women as a tool for inclusive economic growth and development. Criticised by some as a freebie, schemes offering free bus travel to women are becoming increasingly popular, with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay last week expanding the scheme in the state by removing the limit on daily trips. The expansion is expected to benefit over 84 lakh women. Some of the other states that offer free bus rides to women include Delhi, Punjab, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, West Bengal and Keralam. MoSPIs survey report released on Monday also showed that the monthly expenditure commuting to work for urban women in many of these states was much lower than in others Rs 564 in Tamil Nadu, Rs 577 in Karnataka, Rs 716 in Andhra Pradesh, Rs 746 in Telangana, and Rs 820 in Punjab. The all-India average for urban women was Rs 884.

articleTitle: Trump approves firing squad execution for 2009 Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Donald Trump, firing Squad, Nidal Hasan
description: Nidal Hasan had opened fire on unarmed troops at Fort Hood, Texas, while shouting "Allahu Akbar", resulting in 13 deaths and 32 injuries
body_raw: The Pentagon announced late on Monday that President Donald Trump has approved death by firing squad for Nidal Hasan, who was convicted for his role in the fatal 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell posted on X that the recommendation came directly from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who will set the timeline and venue for the execution. Recalling the event, Parnell noted that Hasan opened fire on unarmed troops while shouting Allahu Akbar, resulting in 13 deaths and 32 injuries. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come, Parnell stated. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended - and President Donald J. Trump has approved - death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009. He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting Allahu Akbar during the attack. The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come. - Sean Parnell SeanParnellASW October 5, 2026 In a follow-up post, Hegseth echoed the sentiment, writing Justice. FROM THE ARCHIVES  Fort Hood Muslims voice outrage at rampage Is firing squad legal in the US? Execution by firing squad is authorised in five US states - Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. Three executions by firing squad were carried out by South Carolina after the inmates chose the method in 2025. Before that, a firing squad execution was carried out in 2010 in Utah. In the United States, a firing squad execution involves strapping the condemned inmate to a specialised chair with protective restraints and placing a dark hood over their head. A medical examiner or official locates the inmates heart and pins a target often a white cloth target with a red bullseye directly over it. The execution takes place behind a wall equipped with small ports or a black curtain, says the Death Penalty Information Center in the US. A team of designated executioners - typically five trained law enforcement or correctional officers - stand roughly 20 feet away armed with identical high-powered rifles. To spare the officers from individual guilt, one of the rifles is randomly loaded with a blank or dummy cartridge so no shooter knows who fired the lethal rounds. Upon command, the shooters fire simultaneously at the chest target, causing rapid fatal internal injuries. Apart from the US, execution by firing squad remains legally authorised as a primary or secondary form of capital punishment in several nations, including Indonesia, North Korea, Taiwan, Cuba, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Yemen, Somalia, and Saudi Arabia. Some countries, like Brazil and El Salvador, authorise firing squad executions during times of military conflict. Firing squad executions in the five states require the Presidents authorisation, as in the Nidal Hasan case. From the archives  OPINION What should we make of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan,who apparently killed 13 innocent people at Fort Hood? The Nidal Hasan Case On November 5, 2009, US. Army Major Nidal Hasan, an American citizen of Jordanian descent, carried out a deadly mass shooting at the Soldier Readiness Processing Center inside the Fort Hood military post near Killeen, Texas. Hasan was a military psychiatrist there. Armed with an FN Five-seven semi-automatic handgun, Hasan opened fire on unarmed troops preparing for deployment, killing 13 people-including a pregnant soldier-and wounding 32 others while shouting Allahu Akbar. The rampage ended when civilian responders engaged him in a gunfight, shooting him multiple times and leaving him paralysed from the waist down. Prior investigations revealed Hasan had been radicalised after getting in touch with extremist Islamic figures, including radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki. Hasan was charged under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and faced a court-martial in August 2013, where he represented himself and admitted to have carried out the attack. He claimed his motive was to protect Taliban leaders abroad. A military jury convicted him on 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder, subsequently sentencing him to death. Since his conviction, Hasan has remained incarcerated on military death row at the United States Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

articleTitle: Harsimrat Badal: ‘I have not signalled Akali Dal, BJP alliance for Punjab polls’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Harsimrat Badal: 'I have not signalled Akali Dal, BJP alliance for Punjab polls'
description: “Our Mawan Dhiyan Insaaf Yatra is about feeling the pain of women who are worst-affected by drug menace in Punjab. Women tell me they are scared to send their children to schools and colleges,” says the lone SAD MP.
body_raw: With the Assembly elections in Punjab just over four months away, Shiromani Akali Dal SADs lone MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal is holding at least three meetings a day as she leads her partys women-focused Mawan Dhiyan Insaaf Yatra against drugs across the state. In an interview with The Indian Express, the four-time Bathinda MP spoke about the drug problem in the state, her partys vision for Punjab, speculations surrounding her entry into state politics, and the buzz about the SAD-BJP alliance, among other issues. Excerpts Your anti-drug campaign, which is focused on women affected by the drug problem, is in contrast to the AAPs Mawan Dhiyan Satkar Yojana. Does this make your outreach difficult? I do not intend to compete with anyone through my programme, which is about feeling the pain of women who are worst-affected by the drug menace in Punjab. Women tell me that they are scared to send their children to schools and colleges. The AAP governments scheme Mawan Dhiyan Satkar financial aid scheme for women is mere symbolism. Instead of providing an aid of Rs 60,000 over a five-year period, they started the scheme just six months before the polls. Women affected by drugs are attending my programmes voluntarily. Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann blames the previous SAD-BJP governments tenure between 2007 and 2017 for the drug problem. When we were in power, drugs were not being sold openly on the streets of Punjab nor were youngsters seen with syringe-poked arms. The AAP is just trying to defame the BJP-SAD tenure but the fact remains that chitta heroin is being sold like toffees in Punjab today. Complainants in cases of drugs are being threatened and punished rather than the suppliers of drugs. We often find policemen accused of selling heroin. There is a nexus between drug suppliers and the police. How can someone who was in power 10 years ago be responsible for todays problems? The CM often takes a dig at Nanhi Chhan, your NGO which also campaigns against drugs. What is your reaction? Nanhi Chhan is very close to my heart. I started it decades ago at a time when I was not involved in active politics. I have empowered over 14,000 women through the NGO. With regard to Manns criticism, what else can I expect from a Guru Dokhi anti-Guru CM, who has not empowered a single woman. His speeches show how much he respects women. While I brought AIIMS to Bathinda, he has not brought a single project for the state during his tenure. What is Mawan Dhiyan Di Fauj campaign that you have now launched? Mawan Dhiyan Di Fauj is to identify drug traffickers and their god-fathers across the state. We will empower our women to become the catalysts of change. I have released a form and it would be distributed in every village. I urge women to fill the form. and become active volunteers in this movement. Women should record all acts of drug trafficking around them with names of the traffickers and peddlers as well as those who were patronising them. The forms would be forwarded to a special anti-drug task force headed by a woman DGP for speedy action against the culprits when the SAD govt will come to power. What is your response to the buzz that your political activity has increased in Punjab as you may enter state politics and could be projected as the SADs CM face? These are rumours being spread by our rivals. I have always been in the state as I belong to a regional party. We understand the pain of Punjab and Punjabis. This is my state. So far, I have covered 14 Assembly constituencies through my yatra and will cover more in the coming weeks. What are your views on the possible alliance between the SAD and the BJP for the Punjab elections? Contrary to perception, I have not given any indication about this possible alliance. When asked in August by our constituency in-charge of Longowal about an educational institution in the area, I had just said if the SAD comes to power, the constituency will see development. I was just referring to former CM Parkash Singh Badals abilities to get projects for Punjab through his goodwill irrespective of who was ruling at the Centre. My statement was misinterpreted. How do you see SADs chances in the 2027 Assembly polls? The Congress won in 2017 after being out of power for 10 years. I firmly believe that public support can bring SAD to power this time as people no longer want Delhi to govern them. Ours is a party of Punjabis and for Punjabis.

articleTitle: Best-selling British novelist and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies at 86
articleFeaturedImageAlt: jeffrey archer
description: In a statement, HarperCollins' UK CEO and Archer's editor Kate Elton said: "We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend."
body_raw: Best-selling British novelist and former Tory politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Monday. Archer, whose international literary career spanned decades with over 300 million books sold across 119 countries, was celebrated for fast-paced thrillers like his 1976 debut Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less and the 1979 hit Kane  Abel. His final book, Adam and Eve, is scheduled for release on Tuesday, reported news agency Reuters. Archer featured on the Sunday Times bestseller lists for 14 years and five months and on the New York Times bestseller lists for five-and-a-half years. Archer is also the only author to have held the spot for No.1 Sunday Times bestseller in fiction, short stories and non-fiction. His readers meant everything to him, and just yesterday he met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event at the Leicester Square Theatre in London, HarperCollins said in a statement. According to HarperCollins, the author passed away suddenly and peacefully between writing sessions. He had been actively promoting the project on recent radio broadcasts and was set to present at the Cheltenham Literature Festival this coming weekend. Were all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers - and a true friend, stated Kate Elton, UK CEO of HarperCollins and Archers longtime editor. Speaking about his conversation with Archer over the authors final book, Elton said When he set out to write Adam and Eve he told me from the very beginning that it would be his final novel - he was so excited about the scale of it and told me that if he could pull it off it would equal anything hed previously written, on which basis he couldnt imagine embarking on any future novels. His political career and scandal Born in north London on April 15, 1940, Archer soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, according to the BBC. In 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth. After serving as a lawmaker for five years, he went on to become Conservative Party deputy chairman under then-Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s, the BBC reported. However, his career was equally defined by a dramatic public scandal. In 1987, Archer won a record 500,000 660,450 in libel damages after suing the Daily Star over allegations involving a sex worker. The matter resurfaced in 1999 while he was running as the Conservative nominee for London Mayor. Following allegations from a former associate that he had fabricated evidence, Archer was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice, drawing a four-year sentence. He ultimately served two years, an experience that inspired his book A Prison Diary. The original libel trial achieved notoriety due to remarks made by Mr. Justice Bernard Caulfield while addressing the jury regarding Archers wife, Mary. Remember Mary Archer in the witness box, Caulfield instructed the jury. Your vision of her will probably never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance? Directing his comments to the author himself, the judge remarked Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel? He returned to the House of Lords after being released in 2003 and served until he retired in 2024. With inputs from Reuters.

articleTitle: No membership card, land after promise, holiday firm to pay Delhi man Rs 3.25 lakh
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Holiday provider Delhi State consumer dispute redressal commission
description: The Delhi state consumer commission directed a holiday provider to refund Rs 1.75 lakh and pay Rs 1.5 lakh for mental agony and litigation costs.
body_raw: The Delhi State Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission recently ordered a hospitality and holiday provider chain to pay Rs 3.25 lakh to a man, as it was held guilty of deficiency in service for not issuing a membership card and allotting the promised plot after collecting the payment for a holiday membership scheme. President Sangita Dhingra Sehgal and Member Bimla Kumari were hearing a plea filed by a man who had paid Rs 1.75 lakh to a holiday provider chain for obtaining membership of a scheme which claimed to provide holiday offers, benefits and a complimentary plot on Bombay-Goa Highway. The opposite party holiday provider was deficient in providing its services to the complainant the man, as it failed to render the services and facilities assured under the Mr Cool Global Parivar Life Membership, including issuance of the membership card and allotment of the complimentary plot measuring 2000 sq. ft. at Kolad, Maharashtra, the September 28 order read. The commission further said that the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, came into being in order to protect the interests of consumers who are affected by the acts of the service providers, who in order to attract the consumers, tend to make lucrative offers but when it comes to actually providing the offered services, they take a step back. The man claimed that in April, 2008, he met the business promotion executives of the hospitality and holiday provider chain who were carrying out word-of-mouth business promotion of the scheme at Connaught Place, New Delhi. According to the man, the hospitality chain was providing various services and facilities in the scheme, including Lifetime membership for the member, spouse, and parents for life, and children up to the age of 18 years. Annual subscription of Rs 4,000. Lifelong, transferable, and global membership. 2000 square feet plot at Golf Village, Kolad, Mumbai, situated on the Bombay-Goa Highway, to be registered in the name of the man. Free holiday for 7 days and 6 nights at any of the properties of the chain for 30 years under Resort Condominiums International RCI membership. 3 days and 3 nights holiday for 5 years by paying Rs. 350 per day Food and Beverages charges extra. Five years free membership to RCI-affiliated clubs. Holiday in Goa for 3 nights and 2 days for a couple with one-way air ticket. The man alleged that, lured by the genuineness of the offer and services, he opted for Mr Cool Global Parivar Life Membership at the rate of Rs 2 lakh and paid Rs 1.75 lakh after a discount of Rs 25,000 was given to him. The man was also allotted a membership number. The man contended that he was assured by the holiday provider that he would receive his membership card and other information, brochures, etc., within two weeks so that he could enjoy the benefits of his membership during the summer vacation. However, no membership card was received, and the entire vacation plan made by the man with his family members was ruined. The man stated that he had to face a very awkward situation as he had also included one of his married relatives and their children. The man was forced to file a consumer complaint because even after calling various officials of the holiday provider and furnishing different documents that the provider asked for, he did not receive any satisfactory response, which caused considerable mental anguish to the man and his father. No proof of payment Advocate Ankur Saini, appearing for the holiday provider, argued that the man never applied for or availed any holiday package services under the agreement and that he had failed to place any proof that he had made a payment of Rs 1.75 lakh towards the membership of the holiday provider. The counsel urged that the man had himself opted for the membership after understanding the terms and conditions of the agreement and had paid the non-refundable membership fee. The counsel stated that the complimentary plot was subject to certain terms and conditions, like payment of Rs 20,000 towards registration and other expenses, which were not fulfilled by the man. Not sustainable The state commission noted that the holiday provider failed to issue the membership card to the complainant the man for availing the services and benefits under the said membership. According to the commission, the contention of the opposite party holiday provider that the complainant man was required to pay Rs 20,000 towards registration and other expenses for the complimentary plot and annual maintenance charges for availing the membership benefits, is also not sustainable, as the holiday provider had failed to establish that it had fulfilled its primary obligations under the membership scheme, including issuance of the membership card and allotment of the complimentary plot. The state commission directed the holiday provider to refund Rs 1.75 lakh paid by the man and further pay Rs 1 lakh as cost for mental agony. The holiday provider was also ordered to pay an additional sum of Rs 50,000 to the man as litigation costs. Takeaway The ruling establishes the obligation of holiday provider companies to follow up on their holiday schemes and that the concerns of the consumers must not be ignored, causing them unnecessary inconvenience. For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states and union territories or call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915 for assistance. articleTitle: No Dussehra or Diwali here: Yavatmal’s dry fields leave farmers counting losses
articleFeaturedImageAlt: No Dussehra or Diwali here: Yavatmal’s dry fields leave farmers counting losses
description: ‘Four chief ministers have come from Vidarbha, yet they could not resolve water crisis here’.
body_raw: Last year, by the time Dussehra arrived, cotton had already reached the homes of farmers in Narsapur. This year, with the festival only days away, Ashok Dasreji Landge, 63, is still waiting for the bolls in his fields to open. Dussehra is on 20th and nothing yet, he says. All 16 talukas of Yavatmal district in Maharashtra are experiencing severe drought conditions, all are under the Trigger-1 drought category, issuing orders for 12 key concessions. Kalamb being one of these. Prolonged dry spells and deficient rainfall have left farmers facing severe drought. Fields that could produce 25-50 quintals of cotton in a normal season are yielding estimates of five to eight quintals, while some farmers expect barely 10-25 per cent of normal crop. Landge is part of a 10-member household comprising him and his wife, their two sons, daughters-in-law and grandchildren. He owns seven acres, with the remaining land divided between two sons. His son Swaroop, 36, cultivates six acres. Landge spent around Rs 21,000 per acre and would normally expect five to six quintals of cotton. But this year there is no production, he said. The family has already been forced to sell their livestock. Four cows and two buffaloes were sold for about Rs 60,000 because the animals could no longer be maintained. Landge said insurance policies taken in earlier years have not yielded payments. His crop loan of Rs 2.10 lakh has remained overdue, while his son has an outstanding loan of about Rs 1.10 lakh. The family pledged household utensils to keep the cultivation going. Diwali and Dussehra will come, but we will have to continue according to whatever the situation is, he said. At Dhanodi, 49-year-old Chitaman Vitthal Bhoyar is facing a similar crisis on his 3.16-hectare holding - one hectare under soybean, two hectares under cotton and 16 gunthas under tur. The soybean crop did not develop because of lack of water. In a good year, I would have got about 25 quintals of soybean. This year, I may get only five, Bhoyar said. For cotton, I would have got around 35 quintals. This year, just seven to eight. His cultivation expenditure has reached about Rs 2.75 lakh, while total crop income may be only around Rs 90,000. Pulling out a plant and showing the sparse pods, he said, Look at this. What will come out of this? His elder daughter is pursuing BSc Nursing in Yavatmal. Her fees for two years being Rs 1.25 lakh, of which he has paid about Rs 25,000. He is now considering withdrawing her. I will have to work somewhere, he said. Bhoyar has also had to sell his bullocks. He bought them for about Rs 70,000 but sold them for around Rs 40,000 after fodder became unavailable. Nitin Gangadhar Nagose 34 of Ichora owns five acres and grows only cotton. Last year, he harvested around 25 quintals this year, he expects seven to eight. Even if it rains now, losses wont be covered, he said. With the farm unlikely to provide income through the year, Nagose expects to take up daily wage work. Construction work in a nearby city may be the only possibility. Nagose lives with his wife, two sons and parents. The children do not understand what is happening. they will demand new clothes for Diwali, he said. Behind Nagoses field, Subhash Meshram, 52, and his wife Sumanbai, 48, face another failed cotton crop. Meshram cultivates five acres of cotton and tur. He dug a 35-foot well but there is no water in it. He expects only four to five quintals of cotton this year against about 50 quintals in a normal year. His wife Sumanbai says, Dussehra and Diwali will not be celebrated this time. They have two bullocks and a cow, but managing fodder and water is difficult. Meshram has a crop loan of Rs 1.30 lakh and does not know how he will repay it. At Ichora, Arun Balkrishna Deotale, 55, cultivates 3.5 acres under tur and cotton and expects only about 10 per cent of the expected crop. I can die, I can hang myself from this tree, but what will that achieve? Ramchandra Warhade, 34, who cultivates four acres of vegetables and cotton, fears farmer suicides could increase this year. Vidarbhas condition is very bad. Four chief ministers have come from Vidarbha, yet they could not resolve water crisis here, he said. Sandeep Thakre, 45, of Ichora, whose cotton, soybean and tur have all suffered, has already spent more than Rs 2.5 lakh. Even if we recover what we have invested, that would be enough, he said. How much will the government give us? Rs 8,000 or Rs 15,000? he asked. Warhade added Fertiliser prices have increased. They say subsidy has been given, but prices have gone up by Rs 200-300 per bag, except urea. The Indian Express spotted panchanamas being done on the fields of Kalamb. We have started conducting panchnamas across the area and will complete them as soon as possible and submit the report to the government, tehsildar Abhay Deshpande said. The decision on relief, he said, would be taken by the state government. Sub-divisional magistrate SDM Vikas Kardile said 15-20 water-conservation works were under way in Kalamb. Our priority going forward is water conservation, Kardile said. The administration is planning recharge pits on farm lands and repairs to deteriorated bunds and gates. March and April will be challenging here. This area largely depends on kharif farming, and that itself is lost, he said.

articleTitle: In Nobel Prize for medicine, a single cell, a flash of light, a breakthrough
articleFeaturedImageAlt: A single cell, a flash of light, a breakthrough
description: In awarding the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Hegemann, American neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth and German biophysicist Georg Nagel, the Nobel Assembly has recognised what is effectively a new era in neuroscience.
body_raw: In the beginning was a single cell, instinctively moving towards light so that the business of living may continue. For German photobiologist Peter Hegemann, studying the microscopic alga known as Chlamydomonas in the 1990s, the question was straightforward How did this simple organism respond to light in one-twentieth of the time that it took the human eye to see? The simplicity of the algas biology, it turned out, was the key needed to unlock the complexities of the human brain, from how different organs are controlled to where feelings, memory, even consciousness itself, reside. In awarding the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Hegemann, American neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth and German biophysicist Georg Nagel, the Nobel Assembly has recognised what is effectively a new era in neuroscience. Hegemann, along with Nagel, discovered channelrhodopsin, a protein that enables Chlamydomonas to react to light in half a millisecond - compared to the 10 milliseconds that it takes the human eye to process information. Deisseroth then used it to develop a light switch that can control nerve cells, thus inaugurating the field of optogenetics. The pinprick of illumination that was made by Hegemanns curiosity has since expanded to shed light on neural pathways that could once only be guessed at. Researchers have been able to identify the precise circuits that control functions and behaviours, from why some people develop a greater preference for sugar to how the rhythms of the heart can affect emotions and how the brain stores information about fear, anxiety and depression. It offers hope for a greater understanding of psychiatric and neurological disorders - areas of darkness that could soon become less intimidating.

articleTitle: From India to Global South, a Gujarat water-governance model
articleFeaturedImageAlt: From India to Global South, a Gujarat water-governance model
description: Water access gains momentum in communities equipped with effective local water governance institutions  such as India’s Pani Samitis.
body_raw: New Delhi recently hosted the ninth edition of the India International Water Week under the theme of climate-resilient water management. The talk focused as much on what India has achieved in the last decade as on what comes next - keeping water supply sustainable, using water more efficiently, and treating used water as both an environmental and economic resource. Indias influence in the global water sector has grown substantially. From a country exposed to frequent climate shocks and access challenges to one now preparing for climate extremes such as floods and droughts, it offers lessons for other countries in the Global South. Over the past decade or so, India has designed and implemented some of the worlds largest programmes to improve water governance, rejuvenate rivers, increase access to water and sanitation, and enable community-driven water conservation, protection, and augmentation. And if we pause and take a step back in time, it is important to acknowledge the leadership of then Gujarat Chief Minister Narendra Modis initiatives between 2001 and 2014, a period that served as a laboratory for the water governance reforms that rolled out across India after 2014. These included the design and implementation of the Swachh Bharat Mission, Jal Jeevan Mission JJM, Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Namami Gange, Atal Bhujal Yojana ABY, Per Drop More Crop PDMC, etc. This 25-year journey is documented in our new case study, From Gujarat to India Water Lessons for the World, which traces water governance reforms in Gujarat and India from 2001 to 2026. Drawing on official data, policy and programme records, the literature and consultations with practitioners, the study examines how political leadership and prioritisation, public financing, institutional reform, administrative implementation and community engagement came together to strengthen water security at scale. Its central finding is that water security is as much a challenge of governance and institutions as it is of engineering - and that the Gujarat experience offers a useful lens for understanding the subsequent national journey and its relevance to the Global South. The case study distils four key lessons which, if studied and contextualised appropriately, can prove effective in the coming years and inform water governance in other countries in the Global South Lead with governance, manage the resource and the service together, root action in communities, and build for scale from the start. Lead with governance, not only hardware Political will and institutional strengthening, rather than infrastructure alone, are core to water security. India has developed a framework for putting them into action at scale, called the 4 Ps, which were articulated by PM Modi and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres through the Delhi Declaration in October 2018. The first is political leadership that prioritises water, reflected in initiatives such as universal tap water access, a cleaner Ganga, community-driven groundwater management, and communication campaigns that keep water top of the mind, such as Jal Shakti Abhiyan Catch the Rain. Second, enabling public and private financing for the capital and recurring costs of water governance. Third, developing partnerships between national, state, and local governments community-based organisations, and national and international knowledge organisations, including multilateral development banks like the World Bank. Fourth, ensuring peoples participation in local water decision-making and management, such as communities resolving to make their villages open-defecation free or preparing village-level water security plans. The 4 Ps are worth emulating in any other context or geography. Manage the water resource and the service together Taps and canals will fail if water does not flow. Addressing both water resources development and service sustainability simultaneously and at scale is paramount. Many cities in Africa are growing at a rapid rate, and industrial and irrigation demand will follow, so planning resources and services together now is cheaper than retrofitting later. As Indias experience in recent decades shows, getting ahead of the coming surge in water demand with linked water resources and services plans would help countries gain from these economic shifts with lower risk for water insecurity. A key part of getting ahead of this surge is being forward-thinking on water reuse, especially for non-potable uses, including planned data centres and semiconductor fabrication units. In India alone, the annual market revenue from the sale of treated used water is projected to reach around Rs 73,000 crore by 2047, at current prices. Root water action in community ownership Water access gains momentum in communities equipped with effective local water governance institutions such as Indias Pani Samitis, infrastructure that consistently delivers a high-quality service, and a balance of internal resources and external support. This has been demonstrated through numerous water conservation, harvesting, and recharge programmes. There is a governance linkage across scales to achieve this. As demonstrated in Gujarat during 2001-2014, the Chintan Shivirs helped prioritise water governance among key stakeholders and formulate actionable solutions to design water-related policies aligned with community expectations. A similar approach was replicated at the national level. The recent Departmental Summit on Water organised by the Ministry of Jal Shakti and addressed by the PM in September 2026 is an example. Going big and scaling up The world is off track on SDG 6 to ensure safe drinking water and sanitation for all, and to sustainably manage water resources, used water, and ecosystems by 2030. Estimates suggest an additional 500 billion in annual investment is required. To meet the scale of water governance reforms, infrastructure installation, data collection, and maintenance required for SDG 6, governments and their leaders cannot afford to slow down. Implementation of JJM across the country demonstrates that India can both think big and implement big. The global community can learn from political leadership at the highest level in India about the will, the financing and the institutions to do it at scale. Iyer is a former secretary to the Government of India at the Ministry of Jal Shakti Bassi is a fellow with the Council on Energy, Environment and Water Smith is an assistant professor at George Mason University. Views are personal

articleTitle: From calling for peace in Russia-Ukraine and beyond, Delhi is now working for it
articleFeaturedImageAlt: From calling for peace, Delhi is now working for it
description: Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that, among the proposals Kyiv has received, India’s is the “most comprehensive”; President Putin has said PM Modi “constantly raises the question about putting an end to the conflict” and has “very good ideas”.
body_raw: By all accounts, India has stepped into a more proactive role vis-a-vis the Russia-Ukraine war. Since the conflict began in February 2022, New Delhi has consistently urged restraint, with PM Narendra Modi saying to Russian President Vladimir Putin in September that year that this is not an era of war. Now, Ukraines Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that, among the proposals Kyiv has received, Indias is the most comprehensive President Putin has said PM Modi constantly raises the question about putting an end to the conflict and has very good ideas and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has acknowledged that India has gone beyond advocacy and is talking to both sides. The shift from calling for peace to working for it is welcome. Delhi must build on it. On this front, Indias interests align with those of the world. Strikes on ports and vessels by both Russia and Ukraine, two major grain exporters, have left farmers in both countries vulnerable and increased the risk of a global food shock. Minister Jaishankar referred to this a few days ago when he warned of a major food crisis in the coming months, in addition to the already significant fertiliser shortages caused by conflicts in Eastern Europe and West Asia. The Ukraine war has also disrupted European energy markets, while Indias purchases of Russian oil have strained ties with the US. An end to the war, or even a de-escalation, would ease such pressures. Going forward, Delhi would do well to focus on specific issues such as grain and energy, rather than sweeping questions involving territory or security guarantees. Both sides have immediate and shared interests in these areas, which means something can be agreed upon without first resolving the harder questions. Even if it does not exert as much leverage over Ukraine or Russia as the US and China, respectively, India can demonstrate that it is actively working towards getting the warring parties to talk. A record of even-handed diplomacy would also answer critics who see India as too close to Russia, a relationship that has drawn scrutiny, not least over oil purchases, for nearly five years.

articleTitle: The knock on the Supreme Court’s door
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The knock on the Supreme Court’s door
description: Even as the Election Commission went back on its own record of inclusiveness, even as it shifted the burden of proof on the vulnerable voter and set up a hurdle race at every stage of the SIR, the Court kept giving it the benefit of every doubt. Going ahead, therefore, not just the EC, the Court is also on test .
body_raw: This newspapers investigation that shone a light on the functioning of the Election Commission of India in the context of the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls has raised serious questions. They have to do with a multi-member body, a constitutional authority, shrinking, many a time, into a one-man show, undermining the checks and balances within. More fundamentally, these questions touch the citizens sacrosanct right to shape her own and the nations future through the right to vote. On Sunday, Justice Ujjal Bhuyan framed the issues in all their breadth and gravity. Large-scale disenfranchisement caused by the SIR, he said, is a violation of the Constitution, and detaching the citizen from the right to vote is like taking out the soul from the body. He referred to debates in the Constituent Assembly to underline the transformational vision and the constitutional guarantee. . years of freedom struggle and the revolt against foreign rule made the adoption of universal adult franchise a natural choice and an essential ingredient of democracy. Equal vote with equal value, regardless of identity and social location, was the first step in a new nation to achieve equality. As the Supreme Court takes up cases related to the modalities of the SIR, and the ECs appointment process and functioning, it would do well to listen in to Justice Bhuyans outlining of what is at stake. Former SC judge Rohinton Fali Nariman underlined it Also on Sunday, he said that the SIRs removal of voters put the right to vote, which is at the heart of our democracy, in great peril. These are not just the concerns of two individual judges, they reflect the disquiet the Supreme Court needs to address to repair the damage done by its troubling silence. The citizens fundamental right to participate in the electoral process has to be protected at all costs. But even as the EC went back on its own record of inclusiveness, even as it shifted the burden of proof onto the vulnerable voter and set up a hurdle race at every stage of the SIR, the Court kept giving it the benefit of every doubt. Going ahead, therefore, not just the EC, the Court is also on test. It is welcome, then, that the SC has made it clear that it did not approve of the changes made to Form 6, which made the process of registration of new voters more daunting. It is reassuring, too, that it wants answers from the EC on aspects of the decision-making within. With due respect, the Court must keep asking questions, again and again. It has a formidable record of affirming the sanctity of Article 324 that secures the Election Commission, it should ensure that remains without stain. For, as one its own members said, this is about the soul of the nation.
