articleTitle: Problem with school History books isn’t just the facts. It’s what they aren’t teaching
articleFeaturedImageAlt: history
description: The real issue lies in shifting the emphasis increasingly to lionised accounts of certain periods in history and presenting the past as a set of acts by a variety of actors engaged in religious antagonism. The interrogative character of historical studies is less frequently seen in these textbooks
body_raw: In recent decades, the periodic revisions of Indian school History textbooks have become increasingly tenuous and worrying. From the invention of fictitious narratives to the erasure or inappropriate abridgement of important periods in history, revisions have assumed several questionable forms. The new textbooks tend to present pieces of information that are sometimes contrary to facts, besides contradicting their own statements in some instances. The larger purpose of these textbook revisions is to present a communally informed account of Indias past that conceives of history as a story of antagonistic groups forced to share a geopolitical territory. History is the discipline that tells us how we reached the present and what it meant to live in times when human lives were organised differently. Human lives were transformed by deep-seated processes involving the introduction and increased use of metals, tools and weapons, fire, agriculture, livestock farming, the wheel, alphabets and numbers, money, monumental architecture and more. Ideas, ranging from god, value, valour and hierarchy to justice, equality, democracy and peace, have shaped human lives in profound ways. A lesson in History involves a nuanced understanding of this journey. Do the new History textbooks in our schools live up to this mandate? No, they do not. NCERTs new Social Science textbook for Grade IX, Understanding Society India and Beyond - Part 2, is the latest in a series of contestable textbook revisions. Released last Tuesday, the book putatively aims to equip students with the skills that are needed to grow. and to enhance their analytical, descriptive, and narrative capabilities. As it turns out, there is much to be desired in the book on these counts. Consider the chapter, Indias Long Road to Independence, which is meant to be an account of a decisive phase in Indian history. The chapter turns out to be an assorted set of events presented chronologically. Little is said in it of historical processes that might encourage critical thinking. Colonialism and nationalism are not defined or discussed in conceptual terms, and processes such as the growth of literature, the development of capitalism and the course of constitutional reforms are nowhere seen. There isnt a word on Ripons local self-governance initiative or the Morley-Minto or the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms. The chapter begins with a big question How did a land of diverse geographies, languages and religions come together to challenge and finally end nearly two centuries of British rule? This is precisely the kind of question that encourages critical thinking, but the chapter ends without touching upon any of the issues that the big question flags. Another chapter, Cultural Currents 13th to 17th Centuries, puts off a conscientious reader with its embarrassing big question How did Indian culture endure and continue to grow richer during this period despite invasions and an unstable political context? The chapter states that religious differences between the Islamic invaders and the local population were so striking that there wasnt really a meeting ground in sight for a time. The power of the Bhakti tradition, along with Sufism, allegedly helped India overcome this crisis. The chapter posits that monotheistic Islam and a religion with several schools of thought were marked by a stark difference. A few pages later, it argues that Islams idea of the oneness of god was already present in the Upanishads. One is left wondering what the stark difference was all about This chapter holds that Islamic invasions led to the imprisonment of women and their sale as slaves. As a natural consequence, women began to make their public appearances less frequent. The use of purdah, ghunghat and other forms of veiling are presented in the chapter as an attempt to protect women from the invaders. The 10th-century traveller Abu Zayds words are cited as evidence to the effect that Indian women wore no veil before the advent of Islam. It is, then, mighty uncertain what Rama was referring to in the Pratima, a play attributed to Bhasa, when he told Sita, apaniyataam avagunthanam, remove your veil. And what was Sudraka speaking of in the Mricchakatika when he said that Sarvilaka covered Vasantasena with a veil vasantasenaam avagunthya after she relinquished her life as a courtesan? These arent the only factual inaccuracies in the book. There are several more. But the challenge that such textbooks pose is not with deliberate misrepresentation of facts or contradictory information. A learned class teacher can address these inadequacies in the classroom effortlessly. The real issue lies in shifting the emphasis increasingly to lionised accounts of certain periods in history and presenting the past as a set of acts by a variety of actors engaged in religious antagonism. The interrogative character of historical studies is less frequently seen in these textbooks. Students are told of thousands of soldiers marching, but not how the soldiers were fed or from where they sourced their weapons. Students are told of high-quality steel produced in ancient India but not how the furnaces worked. Students are told of fire sacrifices by the Vedic people, but not told what it took to produce and maintain fire in an age when lighters and matchsticks did not exist. Students are given a checklist of great advances in astronomy but not told what an armillary sphere is and how it worked. Students are told that Bankim Chandra wrote the Anandamath but not told how the schools of the day equipped children to be literate enough to read Bankim. The schools that made Indians literate in the past 200 years have contributed in no small measure to the making of India as we have known it in our lifetime. This important lesson from the past should inform every line that a textbook committee decides to include in a book meant for our schoolchildren. The writer is associate professor of History at IIT Mandi, Himachal Pradesh

articleTitle: Medicine Nobel goes to scientists who can ‘control brain using light’: What their work is
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Medicine Nobel
description: Nobel Prize 2026 in physiology or medicine winners: What are light-gated ion channels and optogenetics? What exactly have the Medicine Nobel winners done, and what is the real-world impact of their work? We explain.
body_raw: Nobel Prize 2026 Medicine Scientists who developed a way to use light to control specific nerve cells in the brain, allowing researchers to study - and influence - how they shape memories, feelings and behaviour, have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The prize was awarded to Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Prize committee said. What exactly have the scientists done, and what is the real-world impact of their work? We explain. First, what are light-gated ion channels and optogenetics? Light-gated ion channels are proteins that act like tiny doors in a cells membrane, but with one special feature light controls whether the door is open or closed. When a particular wavelength of light hits the protein, it changes shape and opens. Charged particles called ions can then flow through the channel. For example, when light hits the human eye, it sets of a reaction that leads to ions moving through the channel as an electric current, travelling through optic nerves to eventually reach the brain. Optogenetics is a technique that lets scientists control specific cells using light. According to the Nobel Prizes official press release, optogenetics has transformed neuroscience from observing and reading brain activity to actively writing into it, establishing a causal link between distributed, genetically specified circuit motifs and behavior, emotion, and cognition. Among the actions the Nobel winners managed to perform using light was a mouse moving its whiskers, and creating the memory of feeling fear in mice who were perfectly safe. Scientists have always been fascinated with the brain The brain is a remarkable organ, and scientists have long wondered how it can control physical functions, govern feelings and memory, and create art. In the 20th century, researchers identified which brain regions govern which bodily functions. However, they could not show that a specific type of nerve cell directly caused a particular feeling or behaviour, so the resulting picture was like a blurry photograph. Francis Crick Nobel 1962 imagined a solution. Nerve signals are extremely fast, so he reasoned that light would be the ideal way to control them. If nerve cells could be made to react to light, neural activity could be controlled. Crick admitted the idea was far-fetched, but perhaps not impossible. An alga that swims towards light In the early 1990s, Peter Hegemann, at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsried, was intrigued by the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas, which could sense light through an eyespot, a tiny orange dot on its cells surface. If the alga was kept on one end of a bowl, and light shone on the other end, it would swim to that side within milliseconds. Hegemann wondered how the eyespot was so much faster than the human eye. His theory was that unlike the human eye, where photoreceptors first register light and then many proteins have to be moved before an electric signal can pass through the ion gate, in Chlamydomonas, the same protein was doing the reception and the passing on. Others were sceptical, since no known ion channel reacted to light on its own. Isolating the protein proved difficult because it became unstable outside the eyespot. Around the turn of the millennium, however, Japanese researchers mapped the algas DNA. Hegemanns group found two genes resembling known light-capturing proteins. Two scientists and a discovery Hegemann contacted Georg Nagel at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt. Nagel injected each gene separately into frog egg cells, which then produced the proteins and placed them in their outer membranes. He found that Hegemanns hypothesis was correct both proteins were ion channels that opened in response to light. They were named channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2, and the second paved the way to optogenetics. It opened within 0.2 milliseconds of a light pulse, letting positively charged ions flow and producing an electrical signal. The two then introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin-2 into human embryonic kidney cells and hamster kidney cells. The cells became light-sensitive and produced electrical signals when illuminated. In 2003, Hegemann and Nagel published their results and proposed the protein as a tool for generating electrical impulses in cells using light. From psychiatric clinic to nerve cells Karl Deisseroth, while studying medicine in the 1990s, trained at a psychiatric clinic. Here, the functions of the brain, and the sufferings of those whose brain worked differently, held his attention. His group then searched for a protein that could trigger impulses in nerve cells. After hearing of channelrhodopsin-2, he asked Nagel for the DNA. Introduced into rat nerve cells in petri dishes, it was produced without apparent problems. Blue light provoked a nerve signal that could pass to other nerve cells. The group published this in 2005. Control in a living brain The method was named optogenetics in 2006, and researchers soon found more light-activated proteins that turn nerve cells on and off. In 2007, Deisseroths group introduced the channelrhodopsin-2 gene into a specific nerve cell type in the mouse motor cortex. A thin optic fibre fed through a small hole in the skull let them control the movement of the mices whiskers. The same year, light shone on a recently discovered cell type suspected of controlling wakefulness woke sleeping mice, confirming the hypothesis. In 2012, with Susumu Tonegawa, Deisseroth activated an engram, the pattern of neural pathways formed when a memory is created. Reactivating the cells that formed a fear memory made mice show fear when not in danger. It was the first demonstration of exactly which nerve cells are necessary for a specific memory. What it has revealed An adult human brain has around 90 billion nerve cells, each with thousands of connections, and cells with entirely different functions can be intermingled. Optogenetics lets researchers separate them. They have identified circuits governing pain, social behaviour, thirst, food consumption, reward, attention, circadian rhythm and fever. The method also works beyond the brain. Deisseroth showed that forcing the heart to work harder can reinforce anxiety, and other researchers found gut cells that explain why some prefer sugar to sweeteners. Towards treatments Optogenetics has deepened understanding of depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, Alzheimers and Parkinsons disease. In ongoing clinical trials for retinitis pigmentosa, a channelrhodopsin-like protein placed in a blind persons retina restored some vision. With light-emitting glasses, the person could discern and grasp objects on a table. Researchers also hope optogenetics could make cochlear implants more precise. As the Nobel Prize websites official press release says, Across cognition, emotion, and movement, these discoveries and applications illustrate a profound shift. Behaviors previously understood as unified phenomena can now be experimentally deconstructed into discrete computational streams. By enabling temporally precise, pathway-specific interventions in intact brains, optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by revealing the causal logic of brain function. But does this not sound potentially dangerous? While most scientific advancements have the risk of potential misuse, optogenetics doesnt exactly mean shining a light and controlling someones brain. Rohit Singh, Assistant Professor in the Departments of Biostatistics  Bioinformatics and Cell Biology at Duke University, USA, told The Indian Express, There are three major technical safeguards. First and most important, optogenetics typically relies on genetically modifying neurons to produce light-sensitive microbial proteins that human cells do not naturally produce. Doing so would require a genetic intervention. Second, when it comes to visible light, the scalp and skull block much of the incoming light, while the light that penetrates is scattered, making precise targeting difficult. Third, changing the activity of specific neurons does not by itself give us the ability to control a persons thoughts or actions. Who are the Medicine Nobel Laureates? KARL DEISSEROTH Born in 1971. He is theProfessor of Bioengineering and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, USA. PETER HEGEMANN Born 1954. Professor of Neuroscience, Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany. GEORG NAGEL Born 1953. Professor of Molecular Plant Physiology, University of Wurzburg, Germany.

articleTitle: ‘Defeating BJP more important’: DMK, Akhilesh Yadav’s UP poll message
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Akhilesh-Yadav
description: "The alliance should win and defeat the BJP. One party getting two or three seats more is not the question. Everybody should stand united to defeat the BJP," said DMK spokesperson.

body_raw: On April 6 this year, popular Bengali actor Koel Mallick took the oath as a Rajya Sabha MP from the Trinamool Congress. The poll setback triggered an implosion in the Trinamool Congress ranks, with leader after leader deserting the partys firebrand chief Mamata Banerjee. Amid the Trinamool meltdown, Mallick resigned as a Rajya Sabha MP on July 16. Shortly after, she met Union Minister Bhupender Yadav at his Delhi residence. And in less than three months, she is on the list of BJP candidates for the Rajya Sabha. articleTitle: Father from Botswana, mother from India: 5 cheetah cubs at Kuno usher in new lineage
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Five cheetah cubs born at Kuno National Park to a Botswana-born father and India-born mother (Image: @byadavbjp/X)
description: The births take India’s cheetah population to 60, of which 41 have been born in the country. The development comes just months after India brought a fresh group of cheetahs from Botswana to strengthen the genetic base of Project Cheetah
body_raw: An Indian-born cheetah has given birth to five cubs at Kuno National Park after mating with a Botswana Cheetah - ushering in the Botswana lineage of Indias cheetah population. KJP21, a 32-month-old female born in India, gave birth to the five cubs on Monday. Their father is a male cheetah brought from Botswana, making the newborns the first representatives of the Botswana lineage to be born in India, Union Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Bhupender Yadav said. The births take Indias cheetah population to 60, of which 41 have been born in the country. KJP21 is the third female cheetah born in India to reproduce, after Mukhi and KGP12. With the arrival of these five cubs, the cheetah population in India has reached 60, including 41 Indian-born cheetahs. Importantly, these cubs also mark the beginning of the Botswana lineage in India, as their father is a Botswana male cheetah - adding a new genetic lineage to Indias growing cheetah population, Union Minister Yadav said. Another historic and joyous milestone for Project Cheetah  KJP21, a 32-month-old Indian-born female cheetah, has given birth to five healthy cubs in Kuno National Park today. KJP21 is the third Indian-born female cheetah to give birth, after Mukhi and KGP12-an important milestone in the emergence of the next generation of Indias cheetah population. With the arrival of these five cubs, the cheetah population in India has reached 60, including 41 Indian-born cheetahs. Importantly, these cubs also mark the beginning of the Botswanan lineage in India, as their father is a Botswanan male cheetah-adding a new genetic lineage to Indias growing cheetah population. Another generation born on Indian soil, adding yet another beautiful chapter to the remarkable story of cheetah reintroduction in India. Heartfelt congratulations to the veterinarians, field staff, managers and everyone associated with Project Cheetah, whose dedication, commitment and tireless efforts have made these moments possible. Welcome to the world, little ones  WildlifeWeek2026 - Bhupender Yadav byadavbjp October 5, 2026 Boost to Project Cheetah The development comes just months after India brought a fresh group of cheetahs from Botswana to strengthen the genetic base of Project Cheetah. Nine cheetahs - six females and three males - arrived at Kuno from Botswana in February this year. They were the third group of cheetahs brought to India, after eight from Namibia in 2022 and 12 from South Africa in 2023. The decision to bring cheetahs from Botswana followed a fresh round of government-to-government discussions that began in December 2024. The Union government formally approached Botswana as it looked to expand the genetic base of Project Cheetah beyond the animals already brought from Namibia and South Africa. Environment Minister Yadav took up the proposal with Botswanas then Environment and Tourism Minister Boipuso Wynter Mmolotsi. Botswana agreed to partner with India after considering the countrys detailed Action Plan for Cheetah Reintroduction. The partnership received a political push during President Droupadi Murmus state visit to Botswana in November 2025. During her visit, Murmu and Botswana President Duma Gideon Boko witnessed the symbolic release of eight cheetahs, captured from the Ghanzi region, into a quarantine facility at the Mokolodi Nature Reserve. The choice of Botswana was significant because the country has one of Africas largest remaining wild cheetah populations. The first batch from Botswana was transported from the Mokolodi Nature Reserve to Gaborone and then flown to India with the assistance of the Indian Air Force before being taken by helicopter to Kuno. After the November handover, the animals underwent quarantine and the two sides worked through the necessary permissions, including export and CITES clearances, veterinary requirements and arrangements for transporting the animals to India. A three-member Botswana delegation, including veterinarians and an anti-poaching expert, subsequently visited both Kuno National Park and Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary and held discussions with National Tiger Conservation Authority officials in Delhi.

articleTitle: Insurer rejects accident claim over ‘alcohol intake history’, widow secures Rs 60 lakh
articleFeaturedImageAlt: chandigarh police salary bank life insurance claim alcohol head constable widow consumer news
description: The consumer commission noted that the deceased was covered under a personal accidental death insurance policy and his death following the 2022 accident was also undisputed.
body_raw: The Chandigarh District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed an insurance company and a bank to pay Rs 60 lakh to the widow of a deceased head constable, after holding that a hospital record mentioning a history of alcohol consumption did not establish that he was under its influence when the accident occurred. Holding a private insurance company liable for wrongly rejecting an accidental death insurance claim of a deceased, a bench of president Pawanjit Singh and member Mohan Sharma also ordered Rs 20,000 to the widow as compensation for causing mental agony and harassment as well as costs of litigation. The insurer was unjustified in repudiating the claim of the complainant on the ground of the deceasedinsured being under the influence of alcohol at the time of the accident, and the same certainly amounts to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice on their part, and the present consumer complaint deserves to succeed, the September 22 order read. The commission noted that the hospitals summary report mentioned the deceaseds history of alcohol consumption but it did not say that he was under the influence of liquor at the relevant time. Needless to mention here that history of alcohol consumption and being under the influence of liquor are not akin to each other, the ruling held. Widow sought accidental death benefit The womans husband was working as a head constable with the Chandigarh Police and maintained his salary account with a leading private bank. Under a Memorandum of Understanding MoU dated October 30, 2021, Chandigarh Police personnel holding salary accounts with the bank were covered by a personal accidental death insurance policy. On July 2, 2022, he met with a road accident while travelling on his scooter and sustained serious injuries. He was initially admitted to SPS Hospital, Ludhiana, and was later referred to GMCH-32, Chandigarh, where he died from his injuries on July 18, 2022. His widow then sought the accidental death insurance benefit under the MoU. However, the insurance company rejected the claim in October 2022, stating that hospital records indicated that he was under the influence of alcohol at the time of the accident. The woman then approached the district consumer commission, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. Fell within policy exclusion Insurer The insurer opposed the complaint, raising objections regarding its maintainability, locus standi, concealment of facts and cause of action. It admitted that the head constable was insured but argued that the policy was subject to its terms and conditions. It maintained that he was not on duty when the accident occurred and that the claim was rejected because he was drunk, which fell within the policy exclusion. The bank argued that its role under the MoU was limited to facilitating and forwarding the relevant documents to the insurer. It stated that the insurer was responsible for deciding the claim and that the claim had already been repudiated by the insurance company. Couldnt prove intoxication The commission noted that the MoU between Chandigarh Police and the bank covered the deceased under a personal accidental death insurance policy. His death following the July 2, 2022 accident was also undisputed. Regarding the mention of history of alcohol consumption in the hospital summary, the order, relying on national consumer commission precedents, held that simply recording alcohol consumption, without scientific or medical evidence such as a blood-alcohol or breathalyser test, was insufficient to establish intoxication. The commission concluded that the insurer was unjustified in rejecting the claim which amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. Takeaway The ruling made it clear that insurers cannot reject accidental death claims solely on a hospital record mentioning alcohol consumption. It reinforces that intoxication at the time of an accident must be established through credible medical or scientific evidence before applying policy exclusions. Consumers facing similar grievances may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states Chandigarh 0172-2700 183 or dial the National Consumer Helpline at 1915 for assistance. articleTitle: India fined 20% of match fees, West Indies 10% as slow over rate in 3rd ODI draws ICC ire
articleFeaturedImageAlt: West Indies' Shai Hope, left, and India's captain Shubman Gill after West Indies' won the third and final One Day International (ODI) cricket match of a series between India and West Indies, in Mullanpur, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. (PTI Photo)
description: The match went on for over nine hours and the length of the game was pointed out by notably by former India head coach Ravi Shastri from the commentary box and by former wicketkeeper-batter Dinesh Karthik on social media.
body_raw: India and West Indies were both fined by the International Cricket Council on Monday for maintaining a slow over-rates during the third ODI in New Chandigarh. The match went on for over nine hours and the length of the game was pointed out by notably by former India head coach Ravi Shastri from the commentary box and by former wicketkeeper-batter Dinesh Karthik on social media. While India have been fined 20 per cent of their match fee, the West Indies were docked 10 per cent of their earnings after being ruled four and two overs short of their required over-rates respectively, once time allowances were taken into consideration. Match referee Prakash Bhatt imposed the sanctions after the match on Saturday. Both captains pleaded guilty to the offences and accepted the proposed sanctions, meaning there was no need for formal hearings, the ICC said in a statement. The charges were levelled by on-field umpires Jayaraman Madanagopal and Sam Nogajski, third umpire Sharfuddoula Ibne Shahid and fourth umpire Virender Sharma. While India finished with a 2-1 win in the series, the West Indies recorded a famous win in the match itself, rewriting the record for their highest succesfull run chase in ODIs. Captain Shai Hope led the way with an unbeaten 162 as West Indies chased down 352. It was the first time since December 2019 that India had lost an ODI match at home against the West Indies. Earlier, India captain Shubman Gill fell after scoring just one run in his domestic home ground, after having scored centuries in the previous two matches. Virat Kohli was out for a golden duck after that, ending his streak of big scores as well. Rohit Sharma then scored a 92 and that was followed by KL Rahuls unbeaten 162 pushed India to a total of 351 The two sides will now turn their attention to the five-match T20I series, which begins on Tuesday in Lucknow.

articleTitle: ‘We get it, Gaitonde’: This Khakee scene justifies Drishyam 3 cop’s obsession with Ajay Devgn

body_raw: As soon as the trailer of Abhishek Pathaks blockbuster crime thriller Drishyam 3 dropped last month, fans of the franchise have been churning out memes of Kamlesh Sawant, who plays Sub Inspector Gaitonde, on how relentlessly obsessed he is with seeing Ajay Devgns protagonist Vijay Salgaonkar behind the bars for murder. Now, the internet has dug out a 22-year-old scene from Devgn and Sawants maiden collaboration to justify their unending beef. Khakee scene justifies Gaitondes obsession with Vijay Salgaonkar The said scene is from Rajkumar Santoshis 2004 cop thriller Khakee, in which Devgn played the chief antagonist, ex inspector Yashwant Aangre. In a key scene, when a bunch of cops are escaping Devgns clutches by getting on to a moving train, Sawants character, also called Constable Kamlesh Sawant, is seen struggling to catch the train and chasing it with all his might. Come on, Kamlesh, Tusshar Kapoors character of Sub Inspector Ashwin Gupte screams as he extends his hand to Sawant from the moving train. However, before Sawant, whos running on the tracks, can get to the hand reaching out, Devgns antagonist shoots him down with a gun, leading to his death, much to the misery of Gupte and other members of the police force, including DCP Anant Kumar Srivastav Amitabh Bachchan. We get it, Gayatonde. We get it skull emoji, posted an X handle, along with the Khakee scene, justifying the Drishyam characters unrelenting beef with Devgn over the years. Drishyam 3 was in the making way before laughing with tears emoji, commented another X user. Finally, the prejudice is justified, wrote another. This is some bond level finding, said a third one. We get it, Gayatonde. We get it   - The Cinprism TheCineprism October 3, 2026 Since Khakee, which was also Sawants acting debut, hes made a career out of playing a police officer. He also played a cop in late Drishyam director Bollywood directorial debut Mumbai Meri Jaan 2008 and 2011 hit action romance Force, 2012 action film Chakradhaar, Nitesh Tiwaris 2014 supernatural satire Bhoothnath Returns, Amin Hajees 2012 psychological thriller Koi Jaane Na, and Irshad Khans 2023 comedy Non Stop Dhamaal. Interestingly, his character was called Gaitonde in Non Stop Dhamaal, and addressed by his real name Kamlesh Sawant in Force and Bhoothnath Returns. He also played a cop in Marathi films like Santosh Ramdas Manjrekars 2009 vigilante film Mi Shivajiraje Bhosle Boltoy and Chandrakant Kanses 2o15 action thriller Dagadi Chawl. Ajay Devgn recognized Kamlesh Sawant on Drishyam set After working briefly with Devgn on Khakee, Gaitonde reunited with him 11 years later on the set of Drishyam in 2015. Much to his surprise, Devgn not only recognized him, but also walked up to him and gave a pep talk. I usually dont go up to superstars and disturb them on shoot days, and rather focus on my characters take, Sawant told Bollywood Hungama recently. One day, Ajay Devgn sir saw me and walked up to me, and said, Kamlesh, tu Khakee mein tha na, main tujhe goli marta hu you were in Khakee right, I shoot you down?. And then he said, Now, everyone around wanted to know who is playing Gaitonde. Lets make the best of his character, recalled Sawant, who also assured Devgn that hed do full justice to the key character. I replied, Nahi sir, iss character ko nibhane ki, nayay dene ki mein puri koshish karunga No sir, Ill try my best to stay true to and give justice to this character. So, that is the kind of legend Ajay Devgn is. He himself walked up to have a conversation with me, and it is a very big deal for a character actor like me, confessed Sawant. While the first two instalments of the Drishyam franchise were adapted from Jeetu Josephs original Malayalam films starring Mohanlal, the third instalment has been written as an original film by Pathak. articleTitle: Pneumonic plague: What to know about the disease after suspected case in Siberia
articleFeaturedImageAlt: plague
description: A lab worker in Siberia died after developing severe pneumonia, prompting medical observation of nearly 200 people. Here’s what to know about pneumonic plague, how it spreads, its symptoms and how it is treated.
body_raw: Around 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Irkutsk in eastern Siberia, Russia, after an employee of an anti-plague institute there died of suspected plague on October 2. According to local reports, Darya Shipilova had broken a test tube containing the plague pathogen. She fell ill with suspected pneumonic plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia, where an outbreak had been reported near the border with Mongolia. A special set of measures was organized and carried out following a case involving an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, who was diagnosed with pneumonia of unknown etiology, Russias consumer watchdog Rospotrebnadzor told the state agency Tass. The watchdog said expanded testing of samples from the patient found no microorganisms linked to her work at the lab. According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute is a major research and public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russias Far East. First, what is the plague? Plague is an infectious disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a zoonotic bacteria that can spread between animals and people. Y. pestis is usually found in small animals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organisation WHO, humans can be infected in one of three ways - the bite of infected vector fleas, unprotected contact with infectious bodily fluids or contaminated materials like being bitten by an infected rat, and the inhalation of respiratory dropletssmall particles from a patient with pneumonic plague. Types of plague BUBONIC PLAGUE Bubonic plague is caused by the bite of a flea infected with Y. pestis. The disease travels through the lymphatic system to the nearest lymph node where it replicates itself. Of the three variants, bubonic plague has proven to be especially deadly in the past The Black Death, the 14th-century plague pandemic, killed more than 50 million people in Europe, according to the WHO - up to one-third of the continents population. Symptoms typically include sudden onset fever, chills, head and body aches and weakness, vomiting and nausea. The lymph node becomes inflamed and painful as a result, and is called a bubo. SEPTICAEMIC PLAGUE In this variant, the Y. pestis bacteria multiply rapidly in the bloodstream and can develop from any other form of plague. Primary septicaemic plague can also occur. Symptoms can range from bleeding under the skin to severe complications, including organ failure, tissue damage, respiratory distress and bleeding under the skin. If left untreated, it could turn fatal. PNEUMONIC PLAGUE Pneumonic plague, which Shipilova was suspected to have, is the most virulent form of plague with an incubation period as brief as 24 hours. Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous, and according to the WHO, invariably fatal if untreated. As the name suggests, it happens when the bacteria enter the lungs and causes rapidly developing pneumonia and other symptoms. According to the CDC, it is the only form of plague that can be spread from person to person by inhaling infectious droplets - also making it the most contagious. However, this disease also enjoys high recovery rates if detected and treated within 24 hours of onset of symptoms. What you should know With the advent of modern antibiotics, which can treat Y. pestis, and improved hygiene and understanding of the disease, plague is now relatively uncommon. However, it remains endemic in several countries. Today, plague is concentrated largely in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar. Between 2019 and 2025, WHO recorded 3,860 suspected cases worldwide, including 2,646 confirmed cases and 423 deaths among the countries reporting confirmed cases. Plague is treatable with antibiotics, and early treatment greatly improves the chances of survival. Untreated pneumonic and septicaemic plague are invariably fatal.

articleTitle: Telangana CEO orders action against Form 7 misuse to delete eligible voters
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Telangana: BLOs are conducting door-to-door distribution of Enumeration Forms for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. (Express File Photo)
description: A Telangana poll official has warned of action against those misusing Form-7 to seek deletion of voters from electoral rolls.
body_raw: The Chief Electoral Officer of Telangana, C Sudarshan Reddy, has issued an order to the Commissioner of the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation, the District Education Officer, Hyderabad, and all collectors and DEOs of districts across the state, asking them to take appropriate action against individuals who submitted Form 7s to falsely delete eligible voters from the electoral rolls during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The CEOs memo, issued on Monday, reads, It has come to the notice of this office that there have been instances of filing bulk applications in Form 7 before the EROs electoral registration officers and it is also alleged that such forms are not genuine. The memo added that officials, including collectors, DEOs and EROs, should take action against the applicants, who have made knowingly false statement or declaration in writing in form 6, 6A, 7 and 8 as per the provisions of section 31 of the Representation of People Act 1950. The memo further states that such action shall be preceded by an inquiry under Rule 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The CEOs instructions come against the backdrop of the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committees TPCC electoral office filing a complaint with the Commissioner of Police, Hyderabad, seeking FIRs over alleged Form 7 misuse. The first alleged instance of bulk Form 7s in Hyderabad surfaced on October 1, 2026, in Musheerabad constituency. Pre-printed applications were allegedly filed by a booth-level agent BLA of the BJP, seeking the deletion of 31 electors, including a Congress BLA and his family members, the Congress claimed. In another case, a pre-printed Form 7 surfaced in Bahadurpura constituency. This, too, was flagged by the TPCC. The third instance brought to the notice of the commissioner was from Goshamahal assembly constituencys booth number 173. In the Goshamahal case, the BLO booth-level officer refused to accept the bulk pre-printed forms, a TPCC leader claimed. The Congress is in power in the state. Speaking to The Indian Express, a BLO who refused to take in pre-printed Form 7s said, I was only doing my duty. I brought it to the notice of the ERO. What is Section 31 Section 31 of Representation of People Act -1950 refers to making false declarations. It reads,  If any person makes in connection with-a the preparation, revision or correction of an electoral roll, or b the inclusion or exclusion of any entry in or from an electoral roll,a statement or declaration in writing which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Rule 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules 1960 pertains to inquiry into claims and objections. As per the rule, The registration officer shall hold a summary inquiry into every claim or objection in respect of which notice has been given under Rule 19 and shall record his decision thereon. The rule further states, At the hearing, the claimant or, as the case may be, the objector and the person objected to and any other person who, in the opinion of the registration officer, is likely to be of assistance to him, shall be entitled to appear and be heard. The registration officer may in his discretion-require any claimant, objector or person objected to, to appear in person before him b require that the evidence tendered by any person shall be given on oath and administer an oath for the purpose.

articleTitle: ‘Dead insect’ in sealed Rs 50 fruit drink bottle, Bombay woman wins Rs 1.25 lakh
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bottle Orange fruit beverage Maharashtra Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission
description: The Maharashtra state consumer commission rejected the beverage company’s technical objections and upheld Rs 1.25 lakh compensation over a dead insect found in a sealed bottle.
body_raw: The Maharashtra State Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission recently upheld a district commissions order that held a beverage company liable for deficiency in service and confirmed a payout of Rs 1.25 lakh to a woman who had filed the consumer complaint in 2012 after she found a dead insect inside a sealed beverage bottle. While dismissing the appeal, Presiding Member Nisha Amol Chavhan and Member Vijay Premchandani said that the beverage companys attempts to defeat a legitimate consumer grievance through technicalities and procedural hair-splitting regarding lab accreditation and typographical errors are unacceptable. The appellant the beverage company is a large-scale manufacturer producing consumable beverages. The standard of care required in bottling plants is absolute. The presence of a dead insect in a sealed beverage is a gross violation of food safety standards and constitutes a severe deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice, the September 30 order read. The state commission further observed that the presence of a macroscopic foreign biological entity is a manufacturing and packaging defect that occurred at the plant, completely independent of the products expiry date. According to the judgment of the district commission, the woman had alleged that she had bought a 1-litre bottle of an orange fruit-based beverage worth Rs 50 along with some other grocery items on October 23, 2011, from a shop, which was one of the authorised sellers for the beverage company. The woman had claimed that when she took out the bottle from the refrigerator to serve her guests, she saw a dead insect floating inside the bottle even before the seal of the bottle was opened. The woman alleged that her guests were shocked and disgusted by the sight and were not able to consume anything for the rest of the evening, because of which she and her family members were embarrassed. On November 2, 2011, the woman sent a legal notice to the beverage company, as a result of which a consumer response co-ordinator of the company visited her home for inspection of the said defective product and admitted after his evaluation that there was a serious and fatal deficiency in service on the part of the company and apologised for the same. The woman stated that she was also asked to share a few photographs of the defective product so that it could be shown to the quality control department and her grievances would be redressed. However, even after following the instructions of the consumer response co-ordinator and issuing a final reminder, there was no response from the company. Consequently, on January 27, 2012, the woman filed a consumer complaint with the South Mumbai district consumer commission. The district commission, by its judgment on August 30, 2018, held the beverage company and the authorised seller liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, ordering them to pay Rs 50 as the refund of the bottle and Rs 1 lakh as compensation for the mental torture. The shop and the company were further directed to pay an additional sum of Rs 25,000 to the woman as litigation costs. The beverage company approached the state commission to appeal against the order of the district commission. Past shelf life The beverage company contended that the district commission had wrongly relied on a precedent involving a solid food item where visual inspection was sufficient and that the lab to which the defective product was sent for testing was not an appropriate laboratory as per law and its report was legally invalid and cannot be relied upon. The company alleged that the woman had unexplainedly delayed sending the bottle for testing until it was past its 4-month shelf life and had initially refused to hand over the bottle to the manufacturer, because of which she prevented a timely scientific testing of the product. As per the order, the woman did not appear before the state commission despite being served notices, and hence the case continued ex parte. Macroscopic object On the allegation that the woman had refused to give the bottle to the company for testing, the state commission stated that we find no fault in the consumers actions. Handing over the primary piece of physical evidence to the very party accused of the manufacturing defect, prior to initiating legal proceedings, would have jeopardised the consumers case. The state commission observed that the appellant contended that the product was tested past its 4-month shelf life. This argument is fundamentally flawed. The expiry of a products shelf life leads to natural degradation, fermentation, or spoilage of the juice it does not spontaneously generate a dead insect inside a sealed bottle. Regarding the objection to the labs visual inspection, the state commission held that the primary mandate for the lab in this instance was to verify package integrity to ascertain whether the factory seal was intact and to confirm the presence of the foreign object. When a macroscopic object like a dead insect is present in a sealed container, the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur the thing speaks for itself is highly relevant. Chemical analysis of the liquid is secondary when the physical contamination of a sealed consumable item is visibly established, and the seals integrity is confirmed. Accordingly, the judgment passed by the district commission was confirmed and upheld. Takeaway The ruling establishes the obligation of companies producing beverages and food items to ensure proper packaging and manufacturing of its products and that the concerns of the consumers must not be ignored, causing them unnecessary inconvenience. For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states and union territories Maharashtra 1800-22-2262 or call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915for assistance. articleTitle: Russian pneumonic plague scare: What it means for India
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The woman reportedly worked at an anti-plague research institute and was said to have had a possible laboratory exposure.
description: Standard antibiotics (such as gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, or doxycycline) cure it very effectively, but timing is critical. Treatment must start within 24 hours of the first symptoms
body_raw: Reports from Russia about the death of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Irkutsk have raised concerns about a possible case of pneumonic plague and prompted questions about whether the disease could pose a wider public health threat. The case has generated particular attention because the woman reportedly worked at an anti-plague research institute and was said to have had a possible laboratory exposure. Russias public health authorities have described the illness as pneumonia of unknown aetiology cause or origin and said testing did not identify micro-organisms associated with her professional activities. People considered potentially exposed have reportedly been placed under medical observation. Nevertheless, pneumonic plague is one of the most serious forms of plague because it affects the lungs and can spread between people through respiratory droplets. For India, the practical clinical message is therefore two-fold There is no reason for public alarm based on the Russian reports alone, but clinicians should recognise the disease quickly if a genuinely compatible case presents. Pneumonic plague is rare, but it is one of the infections in which early recognition and rapid public health action matter enormously, says Dr Jatin Ahuja, infectious disease specialist, Indraprastha Apollo Hospital, New Delhi, explains. What is pneumonic plague, and how does it differ from other forms? This is a severe lung infection caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis. While bubonic plague attacks the lymph nodes causing swollen lumps called buboes and septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, pneumonic plague infects the lungs. It is the only form of plague that spreads directly from person to person through the air. How easily does it spread, and what poses the greatest risk? It does not linger in the air like measles or spread as easily as the flu. It spreads through heavy respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or spits blood. The greatest risk is being within 6 feet 2 meters of a coughing patient without a mask, caring for them directly, or performing medical procedures on their airway. What is the incubation period, and what are the warning symptoms? Symptoms appear quickly, usually within one to three days range one to seven days. It begins suddenly with high fever, chills, severe headache and extreme weakness, rapidly followed by shortness of breath, chest pain, and a cough that brings up watery, blood-tinged, or pinkish phlegm. How effective are modern antibiotics and how fast must they be started? Standard antibiotics such as gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, or doxycycline cure it very effectively, but timing is critical. Treatment must start within 24 hours of the first symptoms. Because lung damage progresses rapidly, delaying treatment beyond the first day dramatically raises the risk of death. What steps do health authorities take after a suspected case? Health officials immediately place the patient in isolated, negative-pressure rooms and wear protective gear N95 masks. They track down everyone who was in close contact, give them preventive antibiotic pills for 7 days, and monitor their temperature twice daily. Sputum and blood samples are rushed to reference labs for confirmation. Is there a risk for people in India right now? The risk is virtually zero. Because people only transmit it once they are visibly very sick, it is difficult for an infected person to travel undetected on long international journeys. For the risk to change, there would need to be widespread, uncontrolled outbreaks spreading through major international transport hubs. How would India detect and handle a symptomatic traveller from abroad? Indias Port Health Organisations screen incoming international travelers at airports. If an inbound passenger falls severely ill, the flight crew alerts air traffic control, and the plane is directed to an isolation bay. The passenger is transferred by a specialized biocontainment ambulance to designated infectious disease hospitals like AIIMS or Safdarjung, fellow passengers seated nearby are traced and given preventive antibiotics, and samples are tested at the National Centre for Disease Control NCDC. Are Indian hospitals prepared to identify it despite common symptoms? Initial symptoms look identical to standard viral flu or pneumonia, which is a diagnostic challenge. However, hospitals ask for recent international travel history for any rapidly deteriorating lung infection. Indian tertiary and government referral centers have standard stockpiles of effective antibiotics ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and established isolation protocols developed during the COVID-19 pandemic. What are the additional clinical points doctors should keep in mind? The most important clinical issue raised by the Russian episode is that pneumonic plague can initially look like much more common respiratory illnesses. Fever, cough, breathlessness and pneumonia are not, by themselves, specific for plague.The epidemiological history can, therefore, become critical. A rapidly deteriorating patient should be asked about recent international travel, residence in or travel to an area where plague occurs, contact with rodents or potentially infected animals, flea exposure, laboratory or occupational exposure, and close contact with a person suspected of having pneumonic plague. That history can change the differential diagnosis and determine whether urgent public-health notification and specialised testing are warranted. Why the Russia story should not be described as an outbreak The Russian reports have generated concern because of the laboratory workers occupation and the possibility of exposure. But unless Russian authorities confirm Yersinia pestis infection and evidence of transmission, describing the event as a pneumonic-plague outbreak would overstate what is currently known.The significance of pneumonic plague lies in its potential for rapid progression and person-to-person transmission - not in evidence that such transmission is currently occurring internationally. What would change the risk assessment for India? The risk assessment would change if there was credible evidence of confirmed pneumonic-plague cases accompanied by secondary transmission, particularly sustained community transmission or clusters across multiple locations.That is different from an isolated suspected case, including one involving a laboratory exposure. How fast does the bacteria mutate? Unlike rapidly evolving RNA viruses, Yersinia pestis does not typically undergo dramatic genetic change over days or weeks. In a suspected pneumonic-plague event, the immediate concern is, therefore, not rapid mutation but whether the bacterium is actually present, whether it is transmitting between people, and whether it remains susceptible to effective antibiotics.

articleTitle: Road closures, diversions, one-way grids: Kolkata’s Durga Puja traffic curbs

description: Here is how to navigate the extensive traffic restrictions in Kolkata during the Durga Puja days.

articleTitle: ‘I buy and send him the bill’: Bhavana and Chunky Pandey on 29 years and modern love
