description: Tamanaah Bhatia and Sidharth Malhotra lauded Kapil Sharma for pulling off roasting without offending anyone, and asked if younger comics are learning from him.
body_raw: On Saturday, the cast of Deepak Kumar Mishras action adventure fantasy film The Vvaan Force of the Forrest, appeared as guests on The Great Indian Kapil Show on Netflix India. The films lead actors - Sidharth Malhotra and Tamannaah Bhatia - couldnt help but heap praises on not only Kapil and his team, but also their co-star Maniesh Paul, for pulling off the art of roasting without offending anyone. Talking about Kapil and Maniesh on the show, Tamannaah said,Seeing you two made me realise hosting is on one side, but you guys are the original roasters. There are a lot of people who roast today, but you do the roast that families can also watch, When she asked Kapil if younger comics have learnt how to roast from them, the comedian quipped, Were observing these younger kids to learn what not to speak so that we dont end up in jail. Sidharth Malhotra also joined Tamannaah Bhatia in praising Kapil Sharma, his team, and Maniesh Paul for keeping comedy clean. Hats off to Kapil and team, and even Maniesh, for doing comedy and roasting in a clean way, for using clean words so that the one its targeted at can laugh instead of getting offended. There are no abuses at all. Thats the USP of the writing of this show, he remarked, as a flattered Kapil accepted the compliments. The Vvaan Force of the Forrest is co-produced by Ekta Kapoors Balaji Motion Pictures and Arunabh Kumars The Viral Fever. Also starring Sunil Grover, Anup Soni, and Shweta Tiwari, among others, it has collected Rs 58.85 crore at the domestic box office within 10 days of release, thus emerging as the fifth highest grossing film of Sidharths career so far. Samay Rainas roast vs Kapil Sharmas comedy Kapil Sharmas cheeky response to Tamannaah Bhatias question on young comics learning roasting from him might be a reference to Samay Raina, who hosts the roast show Indias Got Latent season 2, which also streams on Netflix India along with his YouTube channel. The show was removed from YouTube last year after a controversy following guest and Samays fellow YouTuber Ranveer Allahbadias inappropriate remarks during an episode. That led to three FIRs being filed against Samay, Ranveer, and a couple of others after massive online trolling. Samay took a year-long break from standup comedy before making his return with the special, Still Alive. He announced the return of Indias Got Latent during that show, which kicked off with Alpha stars Alia Bhatt and Sharvari as special guests. Also Read Archana Puran Singhs family, earning more than ever with YouTube, buys another Mumbai villa On Still Alive, Samay also responded to senior stand-up comedian Sunil Pals criticism that he should learn clean comedy from Kapil Sharma, claiming that even Kapil personally expressed his desire to appear on Indias Got Latent before it was forced to go off air. Samay and Ranveer also appeared as guests on a special World Laughter Day episode of The Great Indian Kapil Show earlier this year, when Kapil lauded Samays talent and even got Sunil to forgive both Samay and Ranveer for the controversy.

articleTitle: Missing since July, Premanand Maharaj’s teen disciple traced to another ashram
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Premanand Maharaj's response, urging honesty and compassion, resonated with many for its progressive approach to a sensitive topic
description: Boy’s family staged protest near spiritual guru’s Vrindavan ashram, alleging they were not allowed to see CCTV footage
body_raw: The family of a 17-year-old disciple of Vrindavan-based spiritual guru Premanand Maharaj had been running from pillar to post for nearly three months, seeking information about his whereabouts. On Friday, the family of Anuj Chaudhary, a Hathras district native who had been missing since July, staged a protest near the Shri Radha Keli Kunj Ashram in Vrindavan of Mathura district, alleging the ashram management had been misleading them for the past three months and withholding information about his whereabouts. They later withdrew the demonstration on the assurance of senior police officials. However, their search came to an end on Saturday evening after police said Anuj was traced to an ashram in the districts Barsana area, around 45 km from Vrindavan, where he was believed to have been staying. This came days after a 25-year-old disciple of Premanand Maharaj died after falling from the fourth floor of a building located near the Vrindavan ashram. Anuj, a Class 12 student, took initiation from spiritual leader Premanand Maharaj in July in the presence of his mother. He later returned to his home in Hathras. A few days later, he left home telling his family that he was going to the ashram. But he did not return, said Anujs uncle Nirbhay Chaudhary. The family claimed that they travelled to Vrindavan several times seeking information about Anuj but received no clear response and had filed a missing complaint in Hathras. A case of kidnapping was registered at the Sahibabad police station of Hathras on July 5 in connection with Anujs disappearance. We had been asking the ashram authorities to show us CCTV footage from the premises and from the apartment building where most of the disciples stay, but they did not agree to do so, Nirbhay said. Earlier in the day, police said a preliminary inquiry found that Anuj travelled to Vrindavan in July and took initiation from the spiritual leader. He subsequently returned to his home and later went missing, they said. Anuj is the only son of Rajveer Chaudhary, a farmer. Mathura Senior Superintendent of Police SSP Shlok Kumar said they coordinated with Hathras police to trace him. Circle Officer Sandeep Kumar Singh said during the search for Anuj, police circulated his photograph on social media. A person who recognised Anuj subsequently alerted the police, leading to his recovery, the official added. We will question him to find out where he had been staying since he went missing in July, Singh said. Hathras police have been informed about the recovery, he further said. Meanwhile, the family of a 25-year-old woman from Noida who has been missing since last month approached the Mathura police for help in tracing her. Her family suspects that she might be at the spiritual leaders ashram as she was a follower of Premanand Maharaj and had visited the city in the past. Mathura Circle Officer Sandeep Kumar Singh said the womans family told police that she was a follower of Premanand Maharaj and used to carry his photograph with her. Police claimed that they checked the visitors records of the ashram but did not find the womans name. Also, police are probing the death of 25-year-old Deepak Lodhi, alias Rasik Dulari Sharan, who died after falling from the fourth floor of a building at Guru Kripa Kunj apartment in Vrindavan on September 25. The apartment, where most of the disciples of Premanand Maharaj stay, is located near Shri Radha Keli Kunj Ashram. Police have so far ruled out any foul play, based on their preliminary inquiry and a video that has since emerged. In the video, Deepak Lodhi is purportedly seen sitting on the rooftop for around 11 seconds before suddenly getting up and jumping from the building. No suicide note had been found. Police said they were examining the circumstances surrounding his death. As part of the inquiry, police examined Deepak Lodhis mobile phone and room but said they found nothing that indicated he was facing any problem or what may have prompted him to take the step. Police are awaiting the toxicology report of his blood sample before drawing any conclusions about the circumstances of his death. SSP Shlok Kumar said police are looking into the circumstances surrounding his death.

articleTitle: ‘IIT Guwahati taught me more than engineering: Coffin dances, Maggi and an events head title’ | Life in an IIT
articleFeaturedImageAlt: life in an iit aryan srivastava guwahati
description: Aryan Srivastava is a 3rd-year BTech student in Biosciences and Bioengineering at IIT Guwahati. He appeared for JEE in 2023, scoring 99.2 percentile in Mains; medical reasons derailed his Advanced attempt. He reappeared later, secured AIR 8703 in JEE Advanced, while enrolled at MNNIT Allahabad.
body_raw: - Aryan Srivastava For about eight months in 2023 and 2024, I was living two parallel lives. On the surface, I was a first-year student at MNNIT Allahabad, attending classes, maintaining a decent presence on campus, making sure nothing looked unusual. Underneath that, I was secretly preparing for JEE Advanced all over again, on a schedule I had to hide from almost everyone around me. One wrong conversation and the whole plan would unravel. It worked. In 2024, I secured AIR 8703 in JEE Advanced and got into IIT Guwahati. I am now a third-year student in Biosciences and Bioengineering here. Also Read Half of SC candidates qualify JEE Advanced 2026 as women hit a 6-year high I am a 20-year-old from Prayagraj, and I have performed the coffin dance meme song on guitar for a hall full of professors who had absolutely no idea what was happening. Growing up in Prayagraj My father works in the banking sector, and my mother is a teacher. I am the youngest in the family, which meant my sisters textbooks were always within reach. In Class 7, I found her Class 10 trigonometry books and worked through them because I could not help myself. My father would sit with me when I got stuck on math puzzles, and somewhere in those evenings the shape of my future career quietly decided itself. Read  IIT Roorkee awarded Gold Medal, and it has nothing to do with my CGPA I do not miss Prayagraj, the city. I miss my parents, my sister, and my pet. But Guwahati keeps me occupied enough that homesickness rarely finds a foothold. The first attempt, and what went wrong In 2023, I appeared for JEE Main and scored 99.2 percentile. Then, for reasons entirely outside my control, a medical situation derailed my JEE Advanced attempt. I ended up with an AIR somewhere in the 17,000s, which, for a General category student, earns you a polite pat on the back and exactly zero seat allocations worth considering. I joined Motilal Nehru National Institute of Technology MNIT Allahabad. The college was good, and so were the people. But somewhere inside, I knew I had not finished. Living two lives Taking a partial drop while enrolled at a premier NIT is, to put it mildly, an extreme sport. The challenge was not just the preparation it was the concealment. I had to keep up with MNNIT coursework, appear engaged, maintain a normal social presence on campus, and simultaneously run a JEE Advanced preparation schedule that I could not tell a single person about. The moment anyone found out, the pressure would multiply in ways I did not want to manage. Also Read  Ban gaye tum IITian? Eating pani-puri in Darbhanga, Priyanshu didnt check his JEE result I studied in the margins of the day - before class, after everyone else had gone to bed, and in whatever quiet moments I could find. Some stretches tested everything I had. But having done this once before gave me a sense of what the preparation demanded. I had a map to follow, even if I was still drawing it as I went. In 2024, I reappeared for JEE Advanced and secured AIR 8703. Why Biosciences and Bioengineering? BSBE sits at an intersection of disciplines that appealed to me precisely because it does not trap you in one direction. The engineering foundation it provides is real, but it also leaves room to build on the side software development, machine learning, data analytics. I wanted a branch that would not close doors before I had figured out which ones I wanted to walk through. Arriving at IIT Guwahati I arrived on campus on July 22, 2024. Being the youngest in my family, leaving home for the first time, 1,200 kilometres away, was a bigger deal than I let on. I remember setting up my room, meeting my roommate for the first time, and watching my parents cry as they left. That image has stayed with me. The campus stunned me almost immediately. The lakes, the greenery, the ducklings wandering around like they owned the place. I was genuinely mesmerised. Then, a few days later, I went to Paltan Bazaar, a major market area in the city, and found ducklings on a dinner menu. Also Read  The real skill IIT teaches you is not to study more, but how to focus, be fully present The guitar room I had carried my guitar from home as a stress-relief habit from my JEE mock test days, and it ended up becoming social infrastructure. Within the first few weeks, my room turned into an informal gathering point people would drift in after dinner and stay to listen. I fell ill a few times in those early months, and the same people who had been coming over for the music never left my side when I needed them. That is when I understood that the friendships I was making here were going to last. Clubs, astronomy and the coffin dance meme I initially tried to stay out of clubs. Then the fear of missing out made its case convincingly. I am now part of Anchorenza, the anchoring, public speaking, and content creation club, Equinox, the astronomy club, and TEDxIITGuwahati, among others. I also performed as a guitarist in campus bands and played for Alcheringa, the cultural fest. The most memorable performance was when our band played Astronomia an electronic dance track by Russian artist Tony Igy for an audience of more than 100 people, including several professors who looked genuinely bewildered throughout. We did it entirely because we could. Joining SWB for the gossip, leaving as Events Head I joined the Students Welfare Board primarily to stay informed about what was happening on campus. The inside information pipeline was excellent. What I did not plan for was finding the work genuinely interesting. I eventually sat through a four-hour interview and came out the other end as Events Head. The role pulled me into things I had never expected managing the launch of a new Burger King outlet on campus, drafting 20-page rulebooks for the Sahyog inter-hostel competition and, in January 2026, helping organise and host the Pan-IIT Wellbeing Summit at IIT Guwahati. Coordinating schedules across all the IITs was a masterclass in crisis management - and in learning not to lose your composure in a group chat with 40 people. Taking on that kind of responsibility changes you in ways that are difficult to articulate until you realise you have already changed. On Guwahati The city rewards curiosity. The Brahmaputra in winter, the stillness of it, the way the light sits on the water, is a genuine reset. Fancy Bazar is a cheap alternative to online shopping where you can find duplicates of almost anything at a fraction of the price. Uzan Bazaar has good cafes, though the prices are optimistic for a students pocket. And whatever is open at 2 am becomes, by default, the best food on campus. The campus itself is a 700-acre bubble, separated enough from the city that the culture inside it becomes unusually self-contained. While my friends at city colleges go home after class, IIT Guwahatis real life begins at around 6 pm and has no fixed end time. Looking ahead I want to work at the intersection of technology and business strategy, building products that use software development and predictive modelling to solve real logistical problems. The combination of a BSBE foundation with the technical skills I have been building on the side feels like the right toolkit for it. I have also recently found trading genuinely interesting, so that is something I am following carefully. One thing IIT has taught me - though I would never say this to a professors face - is that engineering is largely the art of learning an entire semesters worth of content the night before an exam. I say this with respect and firsthand experience. But what it has also taught me is that the version of yourself you plan to be when you arrive is seldom the person you actually become. I came to IIT Guwahati with a study plan. I left my first year with a coffin dance performance, an Events Head title I had never intended to hold, and a room that permanently smelled of guitar strings and late-night Maggi. I would not trade any of it.

articleTitle: Neem Karoli Baba film Hanuman Ansh refuses to bow to Drishyam 3, crosses Rs 419 crore mark
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hanuman Ansh box office collection day 58
description: The Neem Karoli Baba biopic Hanuman Ansh's screens were reduced by more than half, but the sleeper hit continues to hold its own in front of Drishyam 3 even in its eighth weekend.
body_raw: Hanuman Ansh box office collection day 58Vishal Chaturvedis devotional film Hanuman Ansh, featuring Shobhinaw Satyaa as revered spiritual guru Neem Karoli Baba, continues to hold its own in front of new tentpole releases at the domestic box office. Its latest threat is Abhishek Pathaks much-anticipated crime thriller Drishyam 3. Even the Ajay Devgn-starrer hasnt managed to slow down the sleeper hit, which is in its eighth weekend. Its now amassed Rs 379.96 crore gross and Rs 321.73 crore net at the domestic box office, and Rs 419.46 crore worldwide. Hanuman Ansh box office collection - Weekend 8 On its eighth Saturday day 58, Hanuman Ansh added another Rs 2.10 crore from 1339 screens to its domestic box office collection, a 6.7 drop from its eighth Friday day 57 earnings of Rs 2.25 crore from 1166 screens. Drishyam 3 did take away most of the holdover releases screens, as the latter earned Rs 2.90 crore from 4345 screens on its seventh Thursday day 56. Given the reduction in screens by more than half, Hanuman Ansh has managed to hold its own in front of a juggernaut like Drishyam 3, which amassed over Rs 66 crore on its opening day at the domestic box office, as per Sacnilk. Given its current momentum, Hanuman Ansh could manage to earn over Rs 6 crore in its eighth weekend despite stiff competition from the Ajay Devgn-starrer. In terms of its domestic net collection, Hanuman Ansh is now just Rs 20 crore away from overtaking Anurag Singhs period war drama Border 2 to become the second-highest-grossing Indian film of 2026. The Sunny Deol and Varun Dhawan-starrer ended its domestic run with a net collection of Rs 341.70 crore. The years highest-grossing Indian film remains Aditya Dhars spy thriller Dhurandhar 2 The Revenge, starring Ranveer Singh, with a domestic net collection of Rs 1,108.90 crore. Hanuman Anshs historic box office run Hanuman Ansh has had an unprecedented box office journey. It released in cinemas on August 7. However, in the absence of any stars and scale, it managed to earn only Rs 25 lakh on its opening day and Rs 1.08 crore in its opening week. It then slipped down to Rs 40 lakh in its second week, facing fresh competition from Independence Day releases - Sunny Deols Batwara 1947 and Emraan Hashmis Awarapan 2. The trajectory changed in the third week when Hanuman Ansh finally crossed the daily threshold of Rs 1 crore on its third Sunday, collecting Rs 2.50 crore. It ended up earning Rs 10.40 crore in week 3, Rs 61 crore in week 4, and 90.25 crore in week 5, snowballing despite competition from tentpoles like Yashs Toxic A Fairytale for Grownups, Akshay Kumar and Saif Ali Khans Haiwaan, Kareena Kapoor and Prithviraj Sukumarans Daayra, Kunal Kemmus Vibe, Ali Fazals Mirzapur The Movie, and Sidharth Malhotras The Vvaan Force of the Forrest. Also Read - Drishyam 3 Box Office Collection Day 2 Live Updates Ajay Devgn film crosses Rs 177 crore mark Hanuman Ansh slipped down to Rs 80.25 crore in week 6, followed by 44.80 crore in week 7. At the conclusion of the eighth week, itll now also release in its dubbed Telugu version, which may further aid its total box office collection. Since its overseas release by Hombale Films on September 11, its earned Rs 39.50 crore internationally.

articleTitle: From kadhi-chawal cart to Mercedes: How a Haryana man sold a Dubai dream
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Dubai
description: Rajesh, who owns of a luxurious farmhouse and drives a Mercedes, operated via a network for duping several people across Haryana: police
body_raw: The food cart that once sustained Rajesh Kumar now lies in a corner of his plush farmhouse, while his Mercedes has been seized. The cart once meant a kadhi and cholle chawal rehri that Rajesh operated till 2019 before his and several others lives changed. Rajesh, aka Nana, entered into an investment network for allegedly duping several people across Haryana. Among those who invested across the state also include well-educated professionals, police said, with complaints lodged coming from Yamunanagar, Kaithal, Karnal, Ambala, and Kurukshetra. The seized Mercedes is in relation to the alleged fraud, which now the police estimates at around Rs 8 crore or above. From inflated digital profits to promises of Dubai flats and plots, the racket allegedly operated through a chain of local fraudsters, with the money trail now being examined by the cybercrime police in Panchkula. The four accused arrested so far are Rajesh and Udham Singh from Karnal, Sushil Kumar from Yamunanagar, and Sanjeev Kumar of Ladwa in Kurukshetra. Recoveries include Audi Q3  Q5, BMW Besides Rajeshs Mercedes, an Audi Q5, Audi Q3 and BMW linked to Sanjeev Kumar and other accused have been seized so far by the police. To recover the proceeds of crime, police have moved court seeking permission to auction these vehicles. At least six electronic devices including Apple MacBooks and iPhones and other mobile phones have been seized, which are now being examined by forensic experts for further collection of evidence. The alleged fraud surfaced when Ashok Kumar, a Panchkula-based government contractor, lodged a formal complaint against Rajesh. I initially did not believe Rajesh and his associates, but they organised an official gathering and said the companys MD and CMD would be coming to the hotel. I also saw Sushil, who introduced me to this fraud racket who initially used to come on a bike, later arriving in an Audi. I started thinking that there must really be profit in this business, Ashok told The Indian Express. I first invested Rs 8,500, and they returned the money to me. Then, in 2021, I took a loan and invested Rs 3.5 lakh. Subsequently, my brothers and other relatives also started investing in the scheme. This way they duped me of 60 lakh. Ashok alleged that more than 20-25 people whom he had brought into the network were eventually unable to withdraw their money despite repeated assurances of profits and repayment. The overall loss suffered by my contacts must be more than around Rs 7-8 crore, he claimed. An FIR lodged in July on Ashoks complaint led to their arrest. Now after two months, the investigation subsequently has widened, with police identifying suspected links to operators based in Dubai who were controlling the entire investment racket. Investors promised of flats in Dubai Among the other individuals who got arrested, Sushil, ran a security agency before 2019. He was arrested from the Delhi airport two weeks ago when he was about to board a flight to Thailand. Udham Singh and Sanjeev, arrested earlier, were unemployed and depended on farming done by family. Investors were shown growing balances on mobile applications and were allegedly led to believe that their money was multiplying rapidly. Through fake mobile apps, the figures displayed on these platforms were manipulated to sustain the illusion of profits and attract more investors. They would rather give their own example, Inspector Yudhveer Singh, SHO, Cyber Crime Police Station, Panchkula, told The Indian Express. In one instance being examined by police, an investment of around Rs 30 lakh was allegedly shown as having grown to Rs 68 lakh in about six months. Ashok alleged that whenever he sought withdrawal of his money, he was told that it had been further invested in cryptocurrency and other schemes. According to the police officials, investors were repeatedly told that Dubai flats had been booked for them, while the applications showed inflated returns. The accused subsequently introduced crypto-related schemes and persuaded investors to shift their money from one platform to another on assurances of higher returns. The police investigation centres on platforms and schemes allegedly operating under names including Bloom Drive, LPNT Cryptocurrency, MSVP Meta Soil Verse Plan, SOIL VERSE and Mechai FX. Police officers The Indian Express spoke to said that Rajesh has emerged as a key figure in the investigation. His friend Pramod Kamboj, who frequently visited him, allegedly introduced him to an online portal, Bloom Company. Rajesh initially invested Rs 7,500 and later around Rs 2 lakh in another platform after Bloom shut down. From there, he took off. He started bringing other people into such money-multiplying schemes, officials said. He attended seminars in Chandigarh, Mohali and elsewhere where people projecting themselves as promoters of such investment schemes explained the investment plans and encouraged investments through meetings and online platforms. Police claimed that Rajesh allegedly received a massive share for bringing in several investors and was later even elevated to the position of Senior Project Head. Rajesh claimed that he was gifted a Mercedes C-class and earned Rs. 2 crore in a short span, a police officer said. A luxury farmhouse and other assets linked to him are being examined as part of the proceeds of crime trail, the officer added. Several accused in Dubai too The investigation has also brought the alleged Dubai connection into focus. Police are seeking the arrest of other suspects including Ravinder Bangar, Satish Mokhra, Devinder Bangar, Karamjeet, B S Randhawa and Happy Sheikh whom the police suspect might have fled abroad. A Look-Out Circular has been issued against Bangar and Sheikh who are believed to be in Dubai, Inspector Yudhveer Singh said. Panchkula Police Commissioner Pankaj Nain has cautioned people against transferring money through online investment, cryptocurrency or stock-trading schemes promising unusually high returns.

articleTitle: In conversation with Gulzar on the home he lost and his ‘longest home’, Mumbai
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Gulzar at his home in Mumbai
description: Veteran poet Gulzar on the home he lost, the city he found and all the words in between.
body_raw: On a day of pelting rain in Mumbai, when the highrises fade into grey silhouettes, a small slope on Nargis Dutt Road in the ritzy Pali Hill leads us to the storied home of one of Indias most definitive modern poets. Boskyana, 92-year-old poet and filmmaker Gulzars home, sits as a quiet haven amid glass and concrete reaching the sky. The raised road, reminder of a city that has been built several times over, has led the quaint white bungalow to live in a somewhat sunken space, somewhat tucked in the past and uninterested in the vertical growth of the frantic world above. As is well known, Boskyana is named after the poets daughter, Bosky filmmaker Meghna Gulzar. What is little known is that she is named after boski, a prized Chinese silk variety known for being soft and delicate. The idea, however, is from another time and place. Gulzars father was a textile trader in Pakistans Dina, an unassuming village located along the Grand Trunk Road in the heart of Pakistans Jhelum district. The poet once joked that if hed had a son, he would have named him Lattha crisp white budget-friendly cotton. It is the warp and weft of this metaphorical silk that runs through Gulzars life, with decades spent spinning language into an artform making the ordinary feel just as fine, weaving those pashmina-like phrases of love and loss Geeli hansi, waqt ke paanv, khwabo ki pudiya, seeli hawa and chand ki bindi wali ratiya, which continue to linger. A large bust of Mirza Ghalib carved in white marble stands guard at one end of the book-lined, exposed-stone wall in the poets living room. A screen divides the study from it. The poets voice drifts in from his book-drowned study - a discussion on the matter of his current iPad. He arrives on the other side in his trademark white, starched kurta pyjama, the frame frailer now, hair a shade greyer. But just as he speaks in that familiar, deep voice, the years seem to melt away. Ive just changed my iPad. And this old cover didnt fit. So a new one needs to be bought, he says, settling on an ottoman. For a writer who has spent decades measuring the weight of ink on paper, it is striking how technology seems to fit seamlessly into this otherwise handcrafted world. Like Online, one of his newer stories, where 11-year-old Suhani is telling her grandfather, Mr Syal, to play Patience on the iPad and not step out during COVID. There is a hint of Gulzar in it. He may be steeped in the rhythms of the past but has embraced the new phases with curiosity. Sitting in Gulzars home that is about half a century old, four days before his 92nd birthday and clutching his latest book Aamchi Mumbai My City in Stories and Poems Harper Collins, Rs 3,999, with English translation by Rakhshanda Jalil, home becomes an obvious subject to open with one that is built and another that is left somewhere and preserved in memory. Gulzars story also has these two homes, ones that have shaped him and his oeuvre, while getting infused into the syntax and cadence of his work. There is one that he left behind in Dina during a bloody Partition, the home that has been a constant refrain in his writing, including Raavi Paar and Footprints on Zero Line Writings on the Partition, among others. It is also a home he didnt revisit for a long time. He couldnt get himself to. His friend Paul Mahindra, who also assisted Bimal da Bimal Roy, told him not to go back. He said something which remained with me. Woh badla huya hoga It would have changed and those images which you are retaining in your head. when you wont find them, toh bohot taqleef hogi. So I did not go. I was about 70 when I went back for the first time, says Gulzar, whose visit was prompted by the hospitalisation of Pakistani poet and journalist Ahmad Nadeem Qasmi. Gulzar often refers to Qasmi as his guru. When I went to Lahore, my friends and I drove to Jhelum. I found my gali bylane soon and it was the same as it was. I visited the primary school where we sat on durries and studied. And suddenly I saw a block named after me. The inscription read Sampooran Singh Kalra urf Gulzar. It was next to another named after Fatima Jinnah. The farmland was gone but someone said of a tree-Ye ped murjha gaya hai, par ye ped abhi tak aapka hai the tree has wilted but it is still yours, says Gulzar, recipient of the Jnanpith Award and Sahitya Akademi fellowship, among numerous other accolades. After Gulzars family moved to Delhi and he was admitted to United Christian School, their house became almost like a refugee camp. People would keep coming from our village. Then my father would keep searching the camps to find anyone of his own. He was affected a lot, says the poet who was packed off on the Frontier Mail to Mumbai that would become the longest home I know, he writes in Aamchi Mumbai. What a strange city this is, and how strangely it rears those who come here. It fights and quarrels. It beats and bruises you. But it also gives you the fondness and affection of a friend. Gulzar writes in Aamchi Mumbai, comprising his impressions about Mumbai - from its Irani hotels, monsoon rain and ocean to its footpaths and people who live on them. When Saleem Sinai, the protagonist of Salman Rushdies Midnights Children, returns to Bombay, he says, Yes, it was my Bombay, but also not mine, capturing a city transformed by time. Does Gulzar, who has spent seven decades in what Rushdie calls the most Indian of Indian cities, feel the same from the time he alighted from the train, a frightened young boy? He sees the change through an unlikely lens the disappearance of Irani hotels from everyday Bombay. Once my toothpaste got over and my elder brother said, go get it from the Irani restaurant. I told him, I need toothpaste, not a pastry. So he told me, for any general store items, go to the Irani hotel, says Gulzar. The leitmotif reappears through his writing on Mumbai. Irani hotel was a complete culture in itself. You could go anywhere in the city and find an Irani restaurant. The North has always had places to drink water a pyau water kiosk or communal tap. In Bombay, Irani hotels put out free drinking water. Then, in chaar aana, I could have my lunch keema pav and tea was a full meal. That is what the Iranis were doing here, says Gulzar, who noticed how leftover food, paid for but untouched, was kept for fakirs, for the poor who would queue up at night for what was called the Irani biryani. Bhookha koi nahi rehta tha No one went hungry. As times changed, all of it got lost somewhere. These hotels and that culture are gone. That is what I miss, says the poet, who adds that in this city, if one is able bodied, they will survive. Aur kuch nahi toh smandar ke kinaare seepiyaan bun kar bhi log guzara karte rahe hain If nothing else, people have managed to sustain themselves simply by gathering seashells along the coastline He recalls the time when Morarji Desai was chief minister and amid prohibition, the clandestine, underground bars emerged. Illicit liquor was available at Pascal ka Adda and Aunty Bars, where alcohol was served with salt to be licked along, says the poet. Characters drinking this illicit liquor often appear in his stories, including in Mez ke Upar, Mez ke Neeche. The way people lived in jhopadpattis, it was full of life. Poverty was there but you never felt ashamed of it. There was a pride and dignity of life to it, says Gulzar. The conversation pauses when old friends Sukhwinder and Jyoti arrive unannounced to wish him ahead of his birthday. The room changes colour, with almost a childlike happiness that takes over Gulzar. Not all of it is to do with the bottle of scotch theyve brought as a present. Aye meri dhee hai, meri maangi huyi beti she is my daughter, my asked-for daughter he introduces Jyoti, also his tennis partner. Giddy, with the rare chance to speak in Punjabi with everyone in the room, he introduces us. This girl is also from Punjab. te Punjabi bol lendi hai she can speak in Punjabi, he tells Jyoti. Like the shade of an old tree, Punjabi occupies a prized place in Gulzars literary life. It is not just his ma boli mother tongue, but one he was encouraged to return to even as he moved through Urdus literary world as a young poet in the Bombay of 50s and 60s. Filmmaker and writer Balraj Sahni, who had also spent time in Santiniketan, would urge him to attend the meetings of the Punjabi Sahit Sabha. Balraj saab told me, Gurudev ne kaya si mainu, madri zubaan ch likh Gurudev had told me to write in the mother tongue, he says. Once in Mumbai, Gulzar lived with his elder brother before moving out and making ends meet by working in a motor garage. The two had their differences. The best part of that motor garage job was that in the time that the paint dried, I could sit and read, says Gulzar, who still regrets having to leave his education at Delhis St Stephens College, where he studied for a few months before joining Khalsa College in Mumbai. But they didnt have Urdu and I didnt want to study Hindi, says Gulzar, who soon moved to National College. Gulzar ended up living in Coover Lodge in Andheris Chaar Bangla, where distinguished writer Krishan Chander lived in the main house. Sahir Ludhianvi rented the first floor and he rented the outhouse for Rs 18 a month. The Progressive Writers meetings were held on Sundays, while the Punjabi Sahit Sabha met on Saturdays. It was at these meetings that literature on social inequality, religious hypocrisy and marginalisation was discussed. Both these associations were very well-knit. Most of the Leftists were there. Poet and lyricist Shailendra was a unionist since he worked in the Railways. As for films, they were never the aim of any of these writers, says Gulzar, who was pushed into films by Shailendra. He would say, achhe khaase writer ho, jaate kyun nahi You are such a competent writer, why dont you go? All these big writers - Ali Sardar Jafri, Krishan Chander, Rajinder Singh Bedi, Sahir Ludhianvi - inki kitaabein padhi huyi hain and then seeing them in person as a young boy was huge, says Gulzar. Another space he frequented was the Bombay Youth Choir. This is how he met composer Salil Chowdhury, founder of the orchestra, who later collaborated with Gulzar on Hrishikesh Mukherjees Anand 1971, among many others. The choir was interwoven with a certain cultural awakening in post-Independence India. In National College, his batchmate was writer Sagar Sarhadi and soon literature became a passion. At that time, if you carried a book on the Russian Revolution, you were considered an intellectual, he says with a chuckle. The two were surrounded by Punjabi writers like Sukhbir, a committed communist, Harnam Singh Naaz, among others. This is when Sagar and I took an oath of sorts we will not take up a job we will only write. Aur nahi hai isme kamai toh dekhenge, says Gulzar. That is how the journey began. People ask me if I was fond of writing since childhood. Its all a myth. Life takes its own time. to adapt your talents and aptitude, he says. He fondly remembers his literary life in Bombays trams. How all of his young writer friends would settle on the upper deck of a tram and continue discussions and recitations as the city rolled past. A one-anna ticket allowed them to ride through the day, so if the discussion continued, so did the journey. From Charni Road to Dadar, hum afsaane sunaate the wed narrate stories. People turned to listen in conductors began to recognise us, knew we would turn up on Sunday. It became so interesting. So this is the city I have spent more than 60 years in, says Gulzar. When American writer Howard Fasts The Naked God came out, explaining why he had left the Communist Party, there was a commotion in our world Howard Fast was the only conversation then. When Faiz would write a nazm from jail, ek leher si daud jaati thi. Wed say, Faiz saab is a very optimistic man, how can he write this. everything was discussed in great detail, he says. Eventually Gulzar found his way into Bimal Roys world. His first screenwriting and lyrics credit came with Bandini 1963. He would go on to make his directorial debut with Mere Apne 1971, about the growing disillusionment among unemployed youth. Decades later, in 2026, its central theme remains relatable. The films that followed - Parichay, Aandhi, Maachis, among others - brought the same literary sensibility to stories of a changing India. As for the songs, his were away from familiar tropes. Gulzar was expanding the vocabulary. Also Read - Gulzar didnt write women to be liked, he wrote them to be understood Not far from Ghalib is a harmonium that RD Burman once brought to Boskyana so that he and Gulzar could experiment with music late at night. The kind of partnership where Gulzar would bring abstract, free-verse poetry, and Burman would somehow compose those into brilliant tunes. The non-rhyming, prose-like lyrics of Mera kuch samaan, tumhaare paas pada hai Ijaazat, 1987 are a fine example of that partnership. Tomorrow you will bring a copy of the newspaper and ask me to make a tune out of it, Burman had told Gulzar before creating one of his most minimalist and haunting melodies. In the poets six-decade career as a lyricist, that song remains a masterpiece that broke every known rule in songwriting. Then there was the equation of the material and non-material - Sawan ke kuch bheege bheege din, khat mein lipti raat. are the belongings a beloved is asking back from her companion. A couple of months ago, he wrote a song for India Ek akela Hindustani, do mile toh Hindustan, a quami tarana a patriotic song for todays generation. The song invokes Hindustan, a term that belongs to an older, more layered vocabulary of the nation. Main sa ki umr mein tha, aur main ni se bhi aage nikal gaya hoon. Ab main upar ka sa ho gaya hoon, he told a few young music students in Kolkata. At 92, Gulzar now has his own musical analogy for age, using ascending notes of the alankaar to describe life. But this upar ka sa may just be the beginning of another octave. After all, he keeps finding words for a changing world. The world where AI may generate Gulzar-like poetry in seconds. But can it live inside those words, or the spaces in between? For that, well always need Gulzar.

articleTitle: Flydubai attacker studied at British university, backed violence against women, Russia’s war
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Flydubai Dubai-Tel Aviv Flight News Live Updates:
description: A Flydubai co-pilot held over an attempted hijacking wrote posts backing violence against women while at a UK university.
body_raw: A day after the alleged attacker on flydubai Dubai-Tel Aviv flight has been identified as Hamam Al-Hammami, fresh details have started to emerge of the Omani national. Al-Hammamis social media posts, especially his stance on women and Russias war on Ukraine, and his extremist views during this study at a British university have now surfaced. During his aviation study at Buckinghamshire New University, Al-Hammamis social media posts backed violence against women and harsh religious punishments. He also backed Russias war in Ukraine. The accused is now in custody in Abu Dhabi. The UAE prosecutor general has called the incident an attempted terrorist attack. Passengers embark on a FlyDubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel. Photo AP This comes days after a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into an emergency on Wednesday, when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain with the crash axe kept in the cockpit. The Boeing 737 Max dropped about 17,000 feet before passengers and crew overpowered the co-pilot, and the plane landed in Saudi Arabia. Since then, the questions have moved from what happened in the cockpit to who the co-pilot is, and how he came to fly passengers. Israels defence minister has described it as a jihadist attack, The Telegraph says. The captain who was attacked, Smit Machchhar, is Indian. What al-Hammamis social media posts show? The Telegraph reviewed more than 2,000 posts from an account that appears to be linked to him, written between November 2021 and August 2022, while he was enrolled at Buckinghamshire New University BNU. The posts backed violence against women and harsh religious punishments. The Independent reports that he earned a distance-learning degree in aviation management at BNU in 2023, and the university says he did no pilot training there. The Conservatives are now asking for tighter checks on international students, including those who study online. The account used the name Pilot Hamam al-Hammami and the handle PilotHamam. Its owner described himself as an Omani civilian pilot from Muscat, and gave details that match al-Hammami, including that his mother is Syrian. According to The Telegraph, the posts include backing for violence against women, support for harsh punishments based on Islamic law, abuse of gay people and sexual insults. In one reply to a woman, the account said it would stomp on her head. In another exchange, about a man who hit a woman, the account compared the act to Russias invasion of Ukraine, which it appeared to praise. The paper says the account also argued that a man accused of blackmailing women should be executed instead of jailed for five years. It cited a Koran passage on offenders being killed or crucified. The Telegraph says these posts were all made while al-Hammami was a student at BNU, which he is believed to have attended remotely from Muscat. A pilot who took the same course at the time told the paper he never met any other student. A former lecturer said al-Hammamis name did not ring a bell, and that many online students do not attend live sessions because lectures are recorded. What does the university say, and why are tighter checks being called for? The Telegraph understands that no one raised a concern or complaint about al-Hammami while he was at BNU. The university has told the paper it will review his time there in light of the material now emerging. A BNU spokesman said the course covered aviation operations, such as mergers, sustainability and finance, and that entry was based on standard requirements. He said pilot training is checked separately, through airport security clearance and airline hiring checks. The university also said it has safeguarding and Prevent policies. A FlyDubai aircraft carrying Israelis who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia is seen parked at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel. Photo AP On the day of the attack, BNU said the Home Office had suspended its licence to sponsor international students over concerns about its compliance. The Home Office and the university both told The Telegraph the suspension had nothing to do with al-Hammami or the attack. The university has 20 days to respond before the licence is revoked. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, told the paper that universities should do more vetting at admission, because people on online courses can still influence others and use their British credentials. Figures from the Higher Education Statistics Agency show BNU had 1,530 students from outside the UK in 2024-25, about 8 per cent of its 18,490 students. What happened on the flight, and what are investigators asking? The Independent reports that about two hours into the flight, al-Hammami took the crash axe and slashed at Captain Machchhar. The plane dropped about 17,000 feet. The Telegraph says Machchhar, though badly hurt, opened the cockpit door so passengers and crew could overpower al-Hammami. The plane landed in Saudi Arabia, in Tabuk. However, al-Hammami allegedly told investigators he meant to crash the plane in Israel. Israeli investigators arrived in the UAE on Saturday to question him. Officials in both countries are trying to learn whether he acted alone or with a network. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said accomplices will pay a heavy price. Some former US diplomats and regional analysts have said the attack may have aimed to damage the 2020 Abraham Accords, The Independent adds. The joint investigation is currently focused on how al-Hammami passed employment background checks. Oman Air previously removed Hammami from flight duties after intelligence officials discovered extremist materials on his devices and noted visits to radical websites, according to reports by The Wall Street Journal and ABC News. It remains unclear whether Omani officials shared these security concerns with neighbouring states or international carriers. The paper adds that supporters of al-Qaeda have used the incident in their propaganda, though no group has claimed it.

articleTitle: Karnataka youth arrested over ‘links’ to Pakistan-based terror and arms networks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Karnataka Police
description: The Karnataka Police and central agencies continue to track the ISI-backed Shahzad Bhatti network, which uses social media to recruit local working-class conduits across states.
body_raw: A 24-year-old college dropout from a remote village in northern Karnataka has become the latest individual arrested in connection with nationwide terrorism cases involving an online conspiracy linked to Pakistan-based operative Shahzad Bhatti. Vishal Kumar Mehtre was arrested at his home in Yenkur village in the Bhalki region of Bidar district Friday. He was produced before a special court for terrorism cases in Bengaluru Saturday and remanded to 14 days of judicial custody. The arrest followed an FIR registered on October 1 at the Khataka Chincholi police station under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act UAPA, 1967, for terror conspiracy, support, and membership of a banned terrorist group after local police received a tip-off about Mehtres online activities. Social media communications point to illegal arms network Police investigation revealed that Mehtre, who dropped out of a Bachelor of Business Administration course, allegedly used social media to communicate with members of the banned terrorist syndicate to procure illegal firearms and arrange arms smuggling. Investigators extracted Instagram and WhatsApp data from Mehtres mobile phone showing direct interactions with Shahzad Bhatti, a government-banned designated terrorist of Pakistani origin. According to the Bidar police, Mehtre communicated with Bhatti associates, including Rana Hunain and Nomi Khan, joined groups suggested by them, and was being linked to illegal arms dealers identified as Ashu Sharma and Raj Bhai alias Lucky Singh. During his court appearance, Mehtre confirmed he was arrested at his house. Despite being a Hindu, this college dropout got pulled into the Bhatti network, a police source said. Broader recruitment pattern across Karnataka Mehtres arrest fits into a broader trend observed across Karnataka in recent months, where several youths, primarily from working-class backgrounds, have been targeted for recruitment through social media by the Shahzad Bhatti network. Previous arrests include Mohammed Sahil, 24, a tea stall owner from Raichur, apprehended in August for plotting civil unrest and communicating with a foreign entity named Rana Bhai for gun trading. Other cases involve migrant workers from Uttar Pradesh, such as construction worker Suhel, 20, arrested in Davanagere after saving a Pakistani number labelled Rana Bhai and joining groups named MEMON and JUTTU-333 and RANABHAI-333. Earlier in June, the Tumkur police arrested Allahbhakash and Zamir Khan for allegedly contacting a Bhatti gang member to mobilise youths and target a Pune-based businessman and right-wing leader. Nationwide crackdown According to the Ministry of Home Affairs MHA, the Shahzad Bhatti network is an ISI-backed, Pakistan-based terror syndicate that pays local conduits to conduct reconnaissance on police, defence, and religious sites, as well as install CCTV cameras for espionage. In August, the MHA reported over 80 FIRs and more than 200 arrests connected to the network, with 253 detentions recorded across 14 states, including Uttar Pradesh 62, Haryana 52, Delhi 51, Punjab 44, and Karnataka 3. Union Home Minister Amit Shah confirmed that law enforcement disrupted the groups plans for subversive attacks, recovering IEDs, grenades with Pakistan Ordnance Factory markings, pistols, live ammunition, and CCTV equipment. Designated a terrorist organisation earlier this year for arms, drugs, and explosives smuggling, the network has also been linked to the emergence of Tehreek-e-Taliban Hindustan and past operational ties with the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.

articleTitle: Gurugram groundwater extraction hits 213% of limit, ban proposed
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The submission called for restoration of identified water bodies, their catchments and feeder channels. (File Photo)
description: The proposals are part of a case that has been before the High Court for nearly two decades.
body_raw: Gurugram is extracting 43,263 hectare metres of groundwater a year against an extractable limit of 20,333 ha m-212.77 of the limit. In view of this, environmental activist and lead petitioner Sunil Singh has proposed before the Punjab and Haryana High Court a complete ban on groundwater extraction, a freeze on new construction without an assured surface water supply and judicial oversight for restoring water bodies. The proposals are part of a case that has been before the HC for nearly two decades. Singh had approached the court in 2008 against alleged rampant and unauthorised tubewell extraction by builders in developing sectors. The case has since involved the wider issue of groundwater depletion and restoration of water bodies in Gurugram. The latest proposals come ahead of an administrative review on October 5 - to be attended by members of the GMDA, HSVP and MCG as well as the petitioners, among others - after a division bench of Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra and Justice Rohit Kapoor described the groundwater situation in Gurugram as grim on October 1. After the court was told that groundwater had plunged to 40 to 50 m across Gurugram, it had noted that annual groundwater extraction in the district was twice the replenishable resource. We expect the authorities to examine the issues threadbare and to suggest appropriate measures as would ameliorate the worsening situation of ground water in Gurugram. It is to be kept in mind that the present generation is only a trustee for the futures to come and if we loose natural resources like groundwater in the manner like it is happening, the future generation would have to face disastrous consequences, the HC had said. In his submission, Singh has said, It is suggested that all groundwater extraction through borewells in Gurugram, whether registered, permitted or unregistered, should be prohibited. All existing borewells should be identified, geo-tagged and sealed in a time-bound manner, and all existing permissionsNOCs for groundwater abstraction should remain suspended during this period. No fresh borewell, renewal of permission or enhancement of the permitted quantity should be allowed. Singh also proposed that no fresh construction be permitted unless authorities demonstrate an assured and sustainable source of water other than groundwater. The submission called for restoration of identified water bodies, their catchments and feeder channels. Citing a GMDA survey that has found 826 of 1,216 water bodies to be retrievable, the affidavit highlighted that 305 existing public water bodies covering about 393 acres and more than 140 natural low-lying water-collection areas covering about 412 acres, which have substantial potential for restoration and groundwater recharge. To overcome administrative delays, Singh proposed that restoration of the water bodies identified in the GMDA inventory be carried out under the supervision of a former judge of the highest judiciary. Further, he proposed a Zero Discharge  Maximum Reuse system. Maintaining that a 300 MLD irrigation network remains underutilised because of sewage treatment shortfalls, the affidavit suggested that no untreated sewage or industrial effluent should be permitted to enter stormwater drains, natural water bodies, open land or groundwater. At present, against a working demand of 770 MLD, GMDA supplies 670 MLD. The remaining 100 MLD is drawn through tubewells operated by the municipal corporation and private builders. The October 5 meeting will examine discontinuing groundwater extraction in areas where GMDA canal supply is available. The administration is to file a compliance affidavit before the HC on October 8.

articleTitle: The morning heart attack pattern: Why the hours after waking may matter
articleFeaturedImageAlt: heart attack
description: Studies have found a morning pattern in heart attacks, but that does not mean there is a single “dangerous” window. Here’s what to know about timing, risk factors and warning signs.
body_raw: A social media claim suggests that most heart attacks happen between 6 am and 8 am. But is there really a specific two-hour window when the heart is most vulnerable? There is some evidence of a morning pattern in heart attacks, but the picture is more nuanced than the 68 am claim suggests. Previous studies have found that acute myocardial infarctions heart attacks occur more frequently between 6 am and noon, rather than specifically between 6 and 8 am. Dr Diwakar Kumar, Consultant, Cardiology Unit-II, Interventional Cardiology, Asian Hospital, explains why this pattern may occur - and why focusing on one particular hour can be misleading. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. Is there really a peak time for heart attacks? Previous studies have shown that heart attacks are more frequent between 6 am and noon, not just between 6 and 8 am, Dr Kumar said. A recent observational study also observed that 31.6 of acute myocardial infarctions occurred between 6 am and noon, he explained. This morning pattern may be related to normal waking changes in the body, including increased sympathetic nervous-system activity, blood pressure, heart rate and changes in clotting, Dr Kumar added. These changes may contribute to cardiovascular stress in people who already have underlying risk factors. However, this does not mean that people are safe from a heart attack outside these hours. This does not mean a person is safe from a heart attack at other times of the day, Dr Kumar said. Is the traditional morning pattern changing? According to Dr Kumar, better control of blood pressure, cholesterol and other cardiovascular risk factors, along with medications such as beta-blockers and other heart-protective therapies, may play a role. People should look at their overall cardiovascular risk instead of one particular dangerous hour, he said. However, Dr Kumar cautioned against concluding that medication has eliminated a morning peak. It would be premature to say medication alone has wiped out a morning peak. Evidence is mixed depending on condition and patient group, he said.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by Mike mikestartegy1 What matters more than the time of day? Dr Kumar highlighted high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, obesity, physical inactivity and a family history of premature cardiovascular disease as important factors. This means that maintaining cardiovascular health involves managing these risks over time rather than simply being cautious during a particular part of the day. Which heart attack symptoms should you never ignore? Chest pressure or discomfort, pain spreading to the arm, back, neck or jaw, breathlessness, cold sweating, nausea, unusual fatigue or light-headedness are signs of a heart attack and require urgent medical attention, Dr Kumar said. What does cardiac arrest look like? The warning signs of sudden cardiac arrest are different. The critical signs for cardiac arrest are sudden collapse, unresponsiveness and no normal breathing or only gasping, Dr Kumar said. If someone suddenly collapses and is unresponsive and not breathing normally, immediate CPR and use of an automated external defibrillator AED, if available, can be lifesaving. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.

articleTitle: Amazon promises more local funding and less secrecy around data centers
articleFeaturedImageAlt: AWS
description: Amazon also tried to separate the anxiety over AI from the debate over data centers.
body_raw: Amazon has become the latest big technology company to promise money for local communities and policy changes in reaction to anti-data-center sentiment that has become a political flashpoint around the country. In a lengthy blog post Friday, the company pledged 1 billion over five years to communities for workforce development, energy efficiency projects and other local priorities. Amazon also said it no longer used nondisclosure agreements with government agencies, a common practice that has created distrust with local residents. Without mentioning China by name, Matt Garman, the head of Amazons cloud computing division, said in the post that other countries were gunning to be at the forefront of artificial intelligence development. More than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the country, he wrote, and if these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations. The tech industry has been on a data center building spree despite intense pushback around the country. The biggest tech companies will spend more than 750 billion on capital expenditures this year, with Amazon the top builder. Some of the facilities are traditional data centers that power online computing. Others, like a flagship Amazon data center in Indiana, have been tailored to the immense computing needs of AI. Other large tech companies have made similar commitments this year. Meta, for example, pledged 1 billion for communities and job training programs, and Microsoft pledged this year to stop using nondisclosure agreements with local governments. Rising local opposition has scuttled or delayed projects and has created a new bottleneck for tech companies looking to build quickly. Data centers have become a hot-button issue in the midterm elections, including in states that have generally welcomed data centers, like Ohio, Texas and Oregon. They have become a particularly difficult problem for Republicans trying to balance local concerns and President Donald Trump, who said the only reason communities would not want data centers was if they want to end up being backwards and poor. Distrust has grown with public fears of AI. A Quinnipiac University national poll released this week found that 71 of Americans would oppose the building of an AI data center in their community, up from 65 in March. Much of Garmans post focused on making the case that data centers are misunderstood. He argued that they used little water - far less than a typical golf course - and that the idea that data centers drive up power costs was misleading because the nations utility infrastructure was overdue for an upgrade. Amazon also tried to separate the anxiety over AI from the debate over data centers, arguing that data centers are the backbone of modern life, powering hospitals and banking systems. Amazons ban on nondisclosure agreements includes its dealings with public utilities. If it is involved in a project initiated by a third-party developer, the company said it would try to avoid having a developers NDA limit what Amazon or a government entity can say about the project. The companys commitments focused almost entirely on communities near data centers and did not wade into the bigger debate around AI safety that has consumed Washington. The Quinnipiac Poll released Wednesday found that most Americans thought AI would do more harm than good, and that almost three-quarters of Americans did not have much or any trust in the leaders of AI companies.

articleTitle: OpenAI safety employee quits, says ‘time for trial and error is over’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: OpenAI says its upcoming Astra model has triggered tougher cybersecurity safeguards because of its advanced capabilities. (Express Image/Agencies)
description: Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what ‌it calls "iterative deployment," releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge.
body_raw: A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the companys approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures. Writing in I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken, published by the Atlantic on Saturday, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being nearly careful enough and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems. The time for trial and error is over, Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation. Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls iterative deployment, releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge. The comments add to a debate within the AI industry over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed, or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly. Robinson, who said he spent 3-12 years at OpenAI, helped draft the companys preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, wrote As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed. Were making sure our models dont become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values.

articleTitle: The silence that makes room for rape
articleFeaturedImageAlt: rape
description: What unsettles the writer is the frequency of hearing violence in a place where others are close by— and how few came forward.
body_raw: I keep returning to an image a woman walking towards a park gate behind her, a man holds out a covered platter. The headline calls him a hungry animal and her his food. I understand the anger, but not the metaphor. A rapist is a man making a choice, and he must answer for it. I was born, raised, and educated in Delhi. Both my parents were born here too. My mothers parents came from Punjab, and my fathers from Uttar Pradesh. I left for New York at 20 and returned when I was 46. I turn 54 in November. Delhi is not somewhere I observe from a distance. It is home. I have spoken against rape in America, in classrooms and at public gatherings. I remember the Cornell case in which a woman accused several men of raping her. It shook that community and stayed with me. A former student has since sued over allegations tied to a 2024 assault they have not been established in court. I kept asking what do people do when they see someone being harmed? Rape is not an Indian crime alone. People compare national statistics, but laws, definitions, and willingness to report differ numbers cannot settle the moral question. What unsettles me is how often we hear of violence in a place where others are close by- and how few came forward. I remember the 2012 Delhi bus rape. A young woman and her friend were attacked by six men on their way home. We came to know her as Nirbhaya. Delhi was filled with candles and anger strangers stood in the winter air and demanded change. Laws changed, but rape did not end. Nirbhaya is not Abhaya, the name used in the 2024 Kolkata case. A woman is a life, not a label in a file. The woman in the image is going somewhere ordinary into a park, into the evening. That catches me. A woman should be able to walk without becoming a warning or a debate about her clothes. The platter is not appetite. It is entitlement dressed up as metaphor. The man holding it is accountable. What troubles me is the publicness of some assaults a street, a bus, a park, with witnesses nearby. Some watch, film or look away. In the worst cases, some join in. Confronting an assailant can be dangerous, but we can call for help, make noise, draw others in, stay with the survivor if safe. A camera is not a conscience. A crowd is not protection if everyone waits for someone else to move. The rapist is someones son, brother, husband, father, uncle, neighbour, classmate, colleague or friend. Violence does not arrive from another species. I have asked in anger what kind of women raise these men. I no longer think that is the right question. A woman is not responsible for the crime of a son, brother or husband. That question shifts the burden back onto women. Women are not the only ones who shape a boy. Fathers, schools, friends, teachers, public figures and courts teach what a man may get away with. A boy who hears that no means try harder, that a girls freedom is an insult, or that male desire is a joke learns a dangerous script. A daughter may be told to return before dark while her brother gets the keys. We are responsible for what we teach and excuse. A sari is not consent No womans clothes cause rape. Neither do her confidence, work, language, independence, or the hour at which she walks. A sari is not consent a short skirt is not consent marriage is not permanent consent. She may drink, dance, change her mind, leave or refuse. If she freezes, goes quiet, fights, or tells someone later, none of that makes the crime hers. Why didnt she fight? is for the person asking, not the survivor. The other day, students at Lovely Professional University protested reports that a woman student had been sexually assaulted on campus. The police registered a First Information Report FIR based on student statements and promised an investigation. But the university called the reports rumours. By evening, the police said they had found no evidence to substantiate the allegation. Facts must be established fairly. Students fear deserves to be heard. Trust is hard to rebuild when young people feel they must block a highway before anyone listens. In Delhi, women students marched after the alleged gang rape of a teenager at Aastha Kunj Park, calling for safer streets and the right to move freely. Reports say Fridays march was moved from Siri Fort Road to Arun Jaitley Park to avoid traffic, where students continued their protest and drafted demands. The march was also a refusal to let womens lives shrink to the distance between a hostel gate and home. They were asking to occupy public space without fear. What does it cost a country when a man convicted of rape can still command followers? Former MP Prajwal Revanna was sentenced to life in one rape case. Asarams life sentence was upheld by the Rajasthan High Court he was later granted parole. Parole is not acquittal, and a sentence is not the same as having served it. Survivors see how long a powerful mans influence can last. The law must be exact. Public memory must be honest. When a politician, teacher, healer, massage therapist, yoga instructor, or godman abuses the trust attached to his role, the harm spreads beyond one woman. It tells others a title or following may count for more than their safety, that rules can bend for a man with influence. This is one cost rape leaves behind a life wounded and trust worn thin. Men and women have been each others companions for generations, standing together through grief, danger and ordinary days. In my classes and public appearances, I return to this subject because we can speak plainly about it. A man who stops a cruel joke, calls for help when a woman is harassed, or refuses to laugh along is doing what friendship asks of him. What should a woman do when she is being raped, harassed, molested, or taken advantage of? In the moment, she does what she can to survive. Afterwards, she deserves belief, protection and care. Ask what the perpetrator must answer for, who will stand beside her, and what must change so she is not left alone with the consequences. I want boys to learn consent I have lived in Delhi and New York. Both places have seen outrage fill a street and fade into routine. I do not want another night of candles followed by the old daylight. I want boys to learn consent before entitlement, witnesses to act, police stations to receive survivors with care, and courts to reach the truth without making a woman relive the crime endlessly. This is the minimum a society owes. I began with the woman walking towards a park. She should not look over her shoulder because a man mistakes freedom for invitation. The man in the image is not hungry. He is accountable. So is the witness who can safely help and chooses silence, and every institution that sends a survivor from one closed door to another. Rape is committed by the rapist. The silence that leaves him room belongs to all of us, and it is ours to break.

articleTitle: Punjabi LGBTQ influencer and makeup artist Mad Sandhu shot dead in Amritsar
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Punjabi social media influencer and makeup artist Madhu Sudan
description: Police say they have some solid leads and will soon crack the case
body_raw: Punjabi social media influencer and makeup artist Madhu Sudan, popularly known as Mad Sandhu, was shot dead by unidentified persons in Amritsar on Saturday, with police saying they have some leads and the accused will be nabbed soon. The incident took place at Loharka Road at around 6 pm, while Sandhu, the son of a retired Punjab Police inspector, was waiting outside a car wash centre for his vehicle. Two unidentified assailants reached there on a motorcycle and opened fire at Sandhu before fleeing the spot, Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Sirivennela said. Around two to three rounds were fired, with an eyewitness claiming that Sandhu was shot at close range. A purported video of the incident showed Sandhu lying in a pool of blood. He was rushed to a private hospital where he succumbed to his injuries, police said. Based on a statement from the family, police registered an FIR and initiated the preliminary investigation. The motive of the attack was yet to be ascertained, a senior police officer said, adding they were working on multiple angles. Deputy Commissioner of Police DCP, Investigation, Amritsar Commissionerate, Prabhjot Singh Virk said, The investigation is currently in its initial stages. We have leads and will solve the case very soon. We have recorded the familys statement. Sandhu used to speak about make-up artistry and gender issues on podcasts and had built a strong digital presence, accumulating around 2.4 lakh followers on Instagram. The make-up artist was also the founder of Mane Lane Unisex Salon in Amritsar and actively operated beauty academies offering courses ranging from self-makeup to professional bridal artistry. Sandhu, who often faced homophobic trolling on his gay identity, would hit back, saying God has made me the way I am, and would remind his audience that if coming from a Jat Sikh family and living in a city like Amritsar, he could achieve success in life, then they too could. His follower base was highly polarised. While admirers supported his creativity, self-expression, and professional artistry by leaving encouraging comments on his tutorials and on his gender-fluid fashion choices, the posts also frequently attracted aggressive online harassment, homophobic trolling, and derogatory commentary questioning his credibility as an educator. A few months ago, an audio-video clip went viral featuring a confrontation between Sandhu and a Nihang Singh, with the latter objecting to the influencers social media activities, cross-dressing choices, and older video reels, warning him to refrain from content deemed harmful to Punjabi culture and youth. Although Sandhu issued a public clarification stating he had changed his content style and stopped repeating past mistakes, he maintained that old clips were being recirculated intentionally to manufacture unnecessary controversy. Congress leader Raj Kumar Verka slammed the AAP government over Sandhus murder, saying the law and order has completely collapsed in Punjab. The AAP government has failed to protect the life of the common man.There is an atmosphere of fear. Meanwhile, Bhagwant Manns government puts up massive hoardings proclaiming a magnificent government and an honest government. It is astonishing that neither Arvind Kejriwal nor Bhagwant Mann said a word about this, he said. Amritsar MP Gurjeet Singh Aujla said Sandhu had been receiving threats for a long time and had openly mentioned these threats on social media as well. Despite this, the government and police failed to take the matter as seriously as they should have, he said, adding that if the threats had been taken seriously in time and necessary security measures had been put in place, perhaps an innocent life could have been saved. Aujla demanded the early arrest of the accused and a thorough investigation into the case.

articleTitle: Government nod for reserved forest status for 112 ha of Ridge, 2,073 ha still unprotected
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The move assumes significance as records show that over 2,073 hectares of encroached forest land in the Capital will remain unprotected even after this first set of notifications is set into effect. (File Photo)
description: This is despite the government making several announcements in recent months to notify several parts of the Ridge as reserved forest.
body_raw: To bolster formal legal protection granted to one of the Capitals most ecologically sensitive zones, the Delhi government on Friday approved the Phase-I notification to declare 112.3 hectares of the Northern Ridge-an extension of the Aravalli range-as a reserved forest under Section 20 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927. However, the government excluded 8.61 hectares of demarcated land from the reserved forest status. The move assumes significance as records show that over 2,073 hectares of encroached forest land in the Capital will remain unprotected even after this first set of notifications is set into effect. This is despite the government making several announcements in recent months to notify several parts of the Ridge as reserved forest. In May, the government declared 673.32 hectares of the Central Ridge as reserved forest. Then, in September, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta announced the approval of a draft notification to declare 400.541 hectares across 15 villages in the Southern Ridge as Reserved Forest. Weeks later, on October 2, a similar Phase-I notification was approved for 112.328 hectares of the Northern Ridge. The exclusions Despite this push, land parcels that were earlier demarcated remain left out from the notifications. For instance, in the Northern Ridge, the Delhi Forest departments approved Working Plan, which was formally sanctioned by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change MoEFCC, records the Northern Ridge area under Delhi Development Authority DDA jurisdiction at 138 hectares. Yet, only 121 hectares were brought to the table for demarcation, and barely 112.3 hectares would make it into the final Phase-I Section 20 notification and be designated as a reserved forest. Similarly, when the Delhi government issued its May 2026 gazette notification for the 991.9-hectare expanse of demarcated land at Central Ridge, it only approved 673.32 hectares under Section 20. Specifically, four pockets within a block were excluded from the notification the Presidents Bodyguard Ground 12.6 ha, an ISRO Earth Station 0.68 ha, the 14th-century Malcha Mahal monument 0.09 ha and a water pump station 0.15 ha. The gazette recorded that these were excluded from Phase-I and will be taken in subsequent phases of notification. Meanwhile, in an affidavit submitted last month to the National Green Tribunal NGT by the Deputy Conservator of Forests PM, defending its phase-wise approach, the Forest department admitted that final notifications under Section 20 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927 are being delayed by a combination of encroachments, pending litigation and incomplete revenue Tatima proceedings. While the 400.541-hectare Phase-II A of the Southern Ridge currently awaits the Lieutenant Governors approval, vast tracts under Phase-II Part B remain entirely unnotified. According to the NGT submission, these excluded land parcels are heavily compromised by village abadis, unauthorized colonies, jhuggi jhopri JJ clusters and religious structures. Furthermore, it stated that these Phase-II B areas are undergoing joint ground re-verification with the Revenue department to determine their legal status.
